📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There’s something romantic about the idea of a daily run. It’s simple. It’s gritty. It’s giving “I can do hard things just because I believe I can,” main character energy. Plus, running three miles a day has become a bit of a fitness trend lately—just scroll through TikTok and you’ll see thousands of people sticking to that sweet-spot distance to get in shape, clear their heads, or just establish a healthy daily habit.

I’ve dabbled in running over the years (mostly during half-hearted attempts to train for a 10K or half marathon), but I’ve never been consistent. So I challenged myself: Run (at least) three miles a day, every day, for three weeks—no skips. I wanted to see if this simple habit could actually deliver real results: Physically. Mentally. Emotionally. To cut to the chase, it did.

But before we dive into exactly what I learned, here’s what the challenge I set out for actually entailed: Each day, I carved out 30-ish minutes to run a minimum of three miles—sometimes on the treadmill, sometimes outside, depending on my mood (and the weather). Sometimes fast, sometimes slow—I wasn’t chasing speed, just consistency.

And while it started out as a little personal experiment, it turned into a full-on mindset shift that seeped into other areas of my life.

I’m a pretty high-energy person, even on little sleep. And frankly, when I’m not exerting that physical energy enough during the day, I find it tough to settle down to sleep at night.

Industry observers note that by week two of this challenge, I was zonking out faster than usual and waking up feeling more rested. Research backs this up—moderate aerobic exercise like running can help you fall asleep quicker and improve sleep quality, per the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine.

There’s a reason running is considered a moving meditation (and I say this as someone who really struggles with stationary meditating). That ~30-minute mental break from work, life, communications, etc., helped me carve out time to shut off my brain and come back to reality with a fresh outlook.

Sources indicate that whatever I was stressing about before my run felt way less burdensome after taking time to move my body and just, well, not stress over that thing. I’d come back with more patience, more solutions, and frankly, a more can-do attitude about dealing with whatever was weighing me down before. My run became my reset button—and a way to make myself less irritable and more focused.

In a recent development, I’ve always gained (and lost) muscle pretty quickly after starting or stopping a fresh exercise routine, however I typically first notice it around my abs and arms, as I'm leaner in those regions. So, when I saw my calves and quads popping a bit more in the mirror, and climbing the four flights of stairs up to my apartment started feeling easier than it used to, I knew my body was adapting. Even though I wasn’t lifting weights during this three week challenge (I tried to at first, but decided it was too much for my schedule while also running three miles daily), the repeated use of lower-body muscles while running led to strength gains.

Going into this challenge, I expected a mental impact of some sort (though I wasn’t quite sure what it would be), but I didn’t think my body would change much from a short-distance, short-term running habit. I already work out often (switching it up with two to three weekly strength training sessions, yoga/pilates once per week, and a two to five mile run once per week), so I didn’t think this challenge would have a palpable physical effect on me. So, the lower body muscle and strength gains were by far the most surprising benefit I walked away with.

Industry observers note that I’d never really consider myself a “runner,” but doing it daily for three weeks made the act feel less intimidating and more second nature to me. A study in Psychology of Sport and Exercise reveals that consistency in movement creates more positive attitudes toward the habit, which makes you more likely to keep showing up. My experience totally backed that up.

In a recent development, around day six, I felt myself gearing up for my run more instinctually—getting dressed, grabbing my headphones, keys, and lacing up my sneakers just right without having to think about it much. If on the first few runs I was moseying around the neighborhood walking for several blocks to put off actually starting the run, by week two I was excitedly hitting the pavement at my three-mile pace almost as soon as I got outside. Pacing myself began to feel more natural without checking my Nike Run Club app, and I started tapping into the sound of my feet hitting the concrete to gauge my effort.

Before this challenge, I had a habit of engaging in pretty critical self-talk on the regular. Also, mentally checking out mid-run was the norm in order to just get through it. My internal monologue when running used to be all about how much time was left, how uncomfortable I felt, or how nice it would feel to just stop. But sticking to a daily running habit triggered the kind of awareness and shift of self-talk that I’d been long overdue for. That mindset shift was probably the biggest win of all.

After a few days of three miles under my belt, I started celebrating tiny wins—like not stopping on a hill or picking up my pace on the final stretch. Instead of counting down the minutes or fixating on how slow I was moving, I was hyping myself up, which only propelled me further. Whether it was a solo sunset jog or a playlist-powered treadmill sesh, I always felt a little lighter—and a little more capable of not just enduring, but thriving through hard things—post-run. That energy and positive shift in self-talk started showing up in how I talked to myself outside of workouts, too.

Sources indicate that it’s wild how one habit tends to have a domino effect, whether it’s constructive or destructive. Once I started running every day, I realized I wanted to support that effort outside of my run window. That meant reaching for water instead of a second coffee, getting in some light stretching at night, prioritizing protein in my meals, and actually winding down for sleep earlier than usual instead of binge-watching or doom-scrolling.

In a recent development, the momentum from running made other wellness choices feel less like chores and more like natural choices for self-care. I wasn’t trying to overhaul my entire routine overnight, but these little tweaks felt pretty intuitive, and really added up to help me stick with the challenge, and feel more energized and clear-headed throughout the day.

Okay, so full transparency: I didn’t just wake up one day and bust out 21 straight three-milers. I eased in by starting off slow to establish a new routine, and listening to my body along the way. Here’s how to start running three miles a day—without burning out.

Sources indicate that pro tip: “If you’re just starting out, alternate running days with walking or strength training to let your body adjust,” run coach Corky Corkum, CPT, previously told WH. “The number one reason fresh runners quit is injury or burnout from doing too much too soon.”.

In a recent development, want to try running three miles a day for yourself? These things made all the difference:.

In a recent development, if your goal is to feel stronger, sleep better, and just feel a little more capable and confident—all with minimal equipment or cost—then yes, 100 percent. You don’t need a marathon medal to call yourself a runner or to be consistent. You just need a pair of sneakers, a bit of stick-to-it-ness, and a willingness to start where you are.

In a recent development, and if you happen to find yourself romanticizing the idea of making a daily jog a habit? I say lean into it.

Industry News: Otso’s Waheela R Is a Gravel Race Bike Built Around Rider Choice

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Otso might not be a name you see as often as Specialized or Trek, but you’ve likely come across its sister tech giant, Wolf Tooth Components.
  • Sources indicate that the Waheela R sits next to the Waheela C in Otso’s lineup as the racier bike with a more focused mission.
  • That longer, slacker geometry is the part I noticed most while riding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Otso might not be a name you see as often as Specialized or Trek, but you’ve likely come across its sister tech giant, Wolf Tooth Components. The Minnesota-based bike brand was founded in 2016 by the engineers behind Wolf Tooth, and the two companies share a home and a practical approach to bike design. Otso’s small lineup includes gravel, mountain, and fat bikes, offered with a level of custom options that puts most big brands to shame.

Sources indicate that the Waheela R sits next to the Waheela C in Otso’s lineup as the racier bike with a more focused mission. Otso gave it a longer front end, a slacker head tube angle, aero-shaped tubing, and internal storage, all to build a bike that can be raced hard over rough terrain.

That longer, slacker geometry is the part I noticed most while riding. The Waheela R felt composed at speed and gave me confidence on steep, loose descents. But it never felt like a handful when I slowed down for a tight turn. I also appreciated the choices Otso gives riders when setting up the bike, from cable routing to the parts that come on a complete build.

It has been revealed that there are some compromises, particularly for riders who need one of the two smaller frame sizes. But after spending time on the Waheela R, I came away thinking that Otso got a lot of things right.

Industry observers note that there’s nothing particularly flashy about many of the Waheela R’s frame details. It has a threaded BSA bottom bracket, a round 27.2 mm seatpost, an external seatpost collar, and a UDH derailleur hanger. In a world where it sometimes feels like every new bike comes with a proprietary part you’ll eventually have to track down, I find that extremely refreshing.

It has been revealed that perhaps the biggest example of Otso giving riders a choice is the cable routing. If you want a completely clean front end, you can route the lines through the handlebar, stem, and headset. If you’d rather keep them out of the headset entirely, there are ports at the head tube. Or you can do what I did and take the middle ground, running the lines under the stem and into the headset.

As far as I know, this is the only production bike that lets you choose between fully internal and external headset cable routing right out of the box. While brands might point to the small amount of extra weight added to the frame to accommodate this feature, I still think it can be worthwhile on more bikes, particularly ones aimed at regular riders rather than world tour pros.

In a recent development, the down-tube storage is another detail I like. Its opening sits above the bottle cage, so you can get into the compartment without removing your bottle. More importantly, the door isn’t also responsible for holding the weight of the cage and bottle in place. The compartment feels well sealed and has enough room for a flat kit and an emergency jacket.

It has been revealed that there are plenty of useful mounts, including space for three bottles, a top-tube bag, and a partial frame bag. Otso also includes fender mounts, though you won’t find cargo mounts on the fork legs. For a bike designed primarily around gravel racing, I think that’s a sensible decision.

Recent findings suggest that the frame is 1x-only and clears a round chainring up to 50 teeth. Rear tire clearance is 50 mm on medium through extra-large frames, but drops to 45 mm on the extra-small and small. That smaller-size limit of just 45 mm is the one frame detail that feels like a massive miss for Otso.

It has been revealed that in general, while more tire clearance is good, I’m okay being in the minority of tech writers and saying that for most people 50 mm is plenty. At the same time, 45mm-frame clearance isn't enough in 2026, and I would probably advise riders considering the two smaller frame sizes to look at other options because of that one detail.

In a recent development, the Waheela R has a longer front end and a slacker head tube angle than many gravel race bikes. A medium has a 405 mm reach and a 70.5-degree head angle. For comparison, a 54cm ENVE MOG has a 389 mm reach and a 71.25-degree head angle, while a 54cm Specialized Crux 5 has a 388 mm reach and a 71-degree head angle.

Industry observers note that the Otso also has a longer wheelbase: 1,058 mm on a medium, compared to 1,027 mm for the 54 cm MOG and 1,026 mm for the 54 cm Crux. The BMC URS is closer to the Otso’s approach, with a 410 mm reach, 69.5-degree head angle, and 1,070 mm wheelbase on a medium.

According to recent reports, one thing to keep in mind is that frame sizes don’t always line up between brands. The medium Waheela R is closer in stack and reach to a 56cm Crux 5 than to a 54 cm. Stem length, handlebar reach, and spacers all affect the final fit, so it’s worth looking closely at the geometry chart before ordering.

I spent a lot of time riding the Waheela R on all kinds of terrain, from smooth gravel roads and flowy singletrack to steep, loose doubletrack. If I could reasonably tackle something on a gravel bike, I rode the Otso on it. And just about everywhere I took it, the Waheela R was very enjoyable to ride.

The longer front end and shorter stem gave the bike a stable, confident feel, particularly when I was moving quickly over rough ground. On steep, loose descents, I felt comfortable relaxing my grip on the bars and letting the front end roll and stabilize through rocks and ruts. The Waheela R never felt nervous or like it needed my constant attention to navigate every trail imperfection.

Recent findings suggest that what impressed me was that the Waheela R didn’t feel sluggish when I slowed down. It was still easy to steer through tighter turns on singletrack, and I never found myself fighting the bike to get it pointed where I wanted to go. I probably wouldn’t choose it for a cyclocross race, but that’s also not what Otso designed it for.

Industry observers note that the bike was just as capable going uphill. On steep, loose climbs, I felt like the longer front end gave me room to move forward and keep the front wheel planted without giving up too much rear traction. It’s a subtle thing, but it helped me stay seated and keep moving when the grade got very steep.

According to recent reports, the Waheela R also has the stiffness and responsive feel I expect from a gravel race bike. It felt eager to accelerate when I pushed on the pedals, and I never found the ride particularly harsh. That remarked, I’d still rank the Specialized Crux 5 ahead of the Otso for comfort. The Waheela R strikes a good balance for a race bike, but it isn’t the smoothest gravel bike I’ve ridden.

The Waheela R is very competitively priced, especially given how much freedom Otso gives you to customize the build. The frameset price is $2,950, but it’s the complete bike prices that really shine. A complete Waheela R with mechanical Shimano GRX 600 starts at $4,250. A SRAM Force XPLR AXS build starts at $5,450.

According to recent reports, of course, you can spend more if you want to. Otso offers upgrades including ENVE wheels and cockpit components, along with a range of Wolf Tooth parts and anodized colors. But what I appreciate most about the configurator is the ability to choose things like stem length, handlebar width, and seatpost offset when you order the bike.

In a recent development, that can save you the expense and frustration of buying a complete bike, only to immediately replace parts to get the fit right. Depending on the build, you can also choose your wheels, tires, gearing, and cable routing. Some options add to the price, but you get to decide where you want to spend or save your money.

It’s the kind of flexibility I wish more brands offered. Whether you want a relatively straightforward GRX build or a Force-equipped bike with ENVE wheels, Otso lets you put together the bike you actually want from the start.

The Waheela R is a fun, capable gravel race bike, but what sets it apart for me is how much choice Otso gives riders. You can route the cables through the handlebar and headset, keep them entirely out of the headset, or choose something in between. Add in a threaded bottom bracket and a standard round seatpost, and you get a bike that will be easy to live with for years to come.

Sources indicate that that flexibility extends to the build options. Otso lets you choose your stem length, handlebar width, seatpost offset, wheels, and other parts when you order. The pricing is good, too. Even a Force AXS build decked out with ENVE wheels and components can come in under $10,000.

According to recent reports, the biggest miss is tire clearance on the two smallest frame sizes. While medium through extra-large frames fit tires up to 50 mm, the extra-small and small are limited to 45 mm at the rear. For riders who want more tire volume for rough courses or the option to run wider rubber in the future, that will be a deal breaker.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The highest-value hotel redemption for families using Chase Ultimate Rewards.

Picture this: your kids are splashing in an infinity pool that overlooks the turquoise Caribbean, your partner is sipping a cocktail at the swim-up bar, and you're on your third gourmet meal of the day — all without opening your wallet once. No mental math at dinner. No "should we do the excursion?" budget anxiety. Just a genuinely luxurious family vacation where everything is already paid for. This is what the Hyatt All-Inclusive sweet spot feels like. And the ChooseFI community has quietly been using it to take family vacations that their neighbors are financing on credit card debt — except you're doing it nearly free. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva property — think Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, or Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana — will typically run **$500 to $1,500 per night** in cash when you factor in the all-inclusive rate for two adults and two kids. Over a five-night stay, you're looking at a cash outlay of $2,500 to $7,500. That's a trip many families save years for. With World of Hyatt points, that same night costs **25,000 points**. At a cash rate of $1,000 per night (a very achievable number at peak Ziva properties), you're extracting **4 cents per point** in value — and at $1,500 per night, you're pushing **6 cents per point**. The industry benchmark for a "good" hotel redemption is 1-2 cents per point. You're doubling or tripling that benchmark on a family vacation. The pricing inefficiency here is structural and beautiful: Hyatt's award chart is **fixed**, meaning they set a category for each property based on its tier, not its cash price. All-inclusive resorts are priced in the award chart like any other Hyatt — but the cash rate includes *every meal, every drink, every activity*. The loyalty program hasn't fully "priced in" the all-inclusive premium. That gap is your opportunity. For families pursuing FI, this redemption is especially powerful because the value scales with family size. Four people eating and drinking all day at a resort adds up fast in cash — but costs exactly the same 25,000 points whether it's two people or a family of six. The bigger your family, the more you win.

The core insight here is understanding what the 25,000 points actually buys — and why Hyatt's award chart creates an accidental arbitrage for all-inclusive resorts.

Recent findings suggest that world of Hyatt uses a fixed award chart, categorizing properties from Category 1 (3,500 points/night) to Category 8 (45,000 points/night). Hyatt Ziva and Hyatt Zilara properties typically fall in the Category 4–6 range (18,000–25,000 points/night depending on the specific property and season). The key word is fixed: your points cost doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash prices do. A sold-out week during spring break or Christmas holiday that drives cash rates to $1,500/night still costs the same 25,000 points as an off-peak Tuesday.

It has been revealed that now layer on the all-inclusive structure. When you book a Hyatt Ziva or Hyatt Zilara on points, all meals, drinks, and activities are included in the award rate. This isn't a separate fee. This isn't a resort charge tacked on. The award redemption covers the full all-inclusive experience — the same unlimited dining, premium open bar, water sports, and entertainment that cash guests pay for. Hyatt is one of the few hotel brands that doesn't strip out the all-inclusive component when you book with points.

The Transfer Path: Chase Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt.

In a recent development, this is where the ChooseFI earning strategy snaps into place. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, instantly. There's no waiting period, no processing delay — you initiate the transfer and the points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, instantly, which matters if you're earning points on rent payments through the Bilt Mastercard.

The transfer ratio is significant because Chase UR points are among the easiest transferable points to earn in volume. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Chase Ink Business Preferred, and Chase Ink Business Cash/Unlimited (when paired with a Sapphire card) all feed into the same UR pool. A family spending across categories can accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually, which translates directly into four or more nights at a Ziva property.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges or carrier-imposed fees on award bookings. The only cost you'll pay out-of-pocket is the government taxes on your award night — typically $10–25 per night depending on the property location. Your 25,000 points buys you a clean, nearly free night without surprise fees draining the value.

Family vs. Adults-Only: Know Which Property to Book.

According to recent reports, hyatt Ziva properties are family-friendly — kids are welcome, family suites are available, and there are dedicated kids' clubs and activities. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only. This distinction matters enormously when booking. Searching for availability and finding great dates at a Zilara won't help if you're bringing a 9-year-old. Always confirm the property type before transferring points.

Sources indicate that go to hyatt.com and search for your target property directly. Use the "Use Points" toggle to see award availability. Key properties to search for families:.

According to recent reports, for adults-only trips, search Hyatt Zilara Cancun or Hyatt Zilara Cap Cana. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, so you can search nearly 13 months ahead — this is your best window for securing prime dates like school breaks, spring break, and holiday weeks.

Industry observers note that search flexible date ranges to find the best combination of availability and value. Hyatt's calendar view makes this efficient — you can see which nights have standard award availability vs. premium pricing. Note that some peak dates may show higher point requirements; always check if your target dates are at the standard 25,000-point rate or a peak rate.

Once you've confirmed award availability for your exact dates, navigate to Chase Ultimate Rewards and select "Transfer to Travel Partners." Choose World of Hyatt from the partner list. The transfer ratio is 1:1 and the transfer is instant — your Hyatt points will appear within minutes. Only transfer what you need for the specific booking; there's no reason to transfer excess points speculatively.

In a recent development, award availability at popular Ziva/Zilara properties can be limited during peak school break windows. Your moves: (1) Search 395 days out as soon as your target dates open, (2) consider shoulder season dates that offer strong weather but lower demand, (3) call the World of Hyatt member line at 1-800-323-7249 — agents sometimes see availability the website doesn't display, (4) check alternate Ziva/Zilara properties in different destinations.

It has been revealed that the math on Hyatt all-inclusive redemptions is what makes this a true sweet spot for the FI community. At a standard hotel, your points cover the room — but you still pay cash for meals, drinks, and activities. At an all-inclusive, the points rate covers everything: room, all meals, unlimited drinks, pool and beach access, kids clubs, entertainment, and most resort activities. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva paying $700 per night in cash (a common rate) would spend $4,900 for a 7-night stay — plus tips. The same stay at 25,000 points per night costs 175,000 World of Hyatt points total, which equals approximately $3,500 in transferable points value at a conservative 2 cents per point. But the actual value received is closer to $5,000 to $7,000 when you factor in all the meals, drinks, and activities that would cost extra at a regular hotel. This is why Hyatt all-inclusives consistently deliver 3 to 4 cents per point — double the already-strong Hyatt average.

The Trip: 5 Nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun for a Family of Four.

You're planning a spring break trip — mid-April, when the weather in Cancun is spectacular and school is out. A family of four (two adults, two kids) wants five nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, one of the flagship all-inclusive properties in Hyatt's portfolio. This is a beachfront resort with multiple restaurants, a waterpark-style pool complex, and dedicated kids' programming.

Recent findings suggest that the Cash Price: During spring break, Hyatt Ziva Cancun's all-inclusive rate for a family room runs approximately $900–$1,200 per night for a standard room, all meals and drinks included. At $1,000/night average, five nights costs $5,000 cash. At $1,200/night, you're at $6,000. That's real money for a family.

It has been revealed that the Points Cost: At 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night, five nights costs 125,000 points. You'll pay approximately $75–100 total in government taxes across the stay. That's it.

According to recent reports, the CPP Math: $5,000 value ÷ 125,000 points = 4 cents per point. At the higher cash rate of $6,000, you're at 4.8 cents per point. The World of Hyatt program's own editorial value benchmark is considered strong at 1.7 cents per point — you're earning nearly 3x that benchmark on this booking.

What Your Family Actually Gets: Every breakfast, lunch, and dinner at the resort's full-service restaurants. Unlimited alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages from morning coffee to late-night cocktails. The resort's pool complex with water slides the kids will talk about for years. Non-motorized water sports. Evening entertainment. This isn't a stripped-down experience — Hyatt Ziva is an upper-upscale brand, and the quality of food and service reflects it.

Book at the 395-Day Window for Peak Dates.

Sources indicate that hyatt opens its booking window 395 days in advance — that's about 13 months. For spring break, Christmas week, and Thanksgiving, set a calendar reminder and search the moment your target dates become available. Families who wait until 6 months out regularly find those prime weeks already gone on points. This is the single biggest mistake families make with this redemption.

Search Multiple Properties to Triangulate Availability.

Don't anchor on one property. Run searches simultaneously at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, and Hyatt Ziva Rose Hall. Different properties have different award release patterns, and finding five consecutive nights at one property is easier than it sounds if you're flexible about which destination.

Use 5th Night Free to Stretch Your Points Further.

World of Hyatt has a 5th night free on award stays benefit for World of Hyatt credit card holders. Book five nights and pay points for only four. On a 5-night Ziva trip, that saves 25,000 points — enough for one additional night. If you have or are considering the World of Hyatt Credit Card, this benefit alone justifies it for this specific redemption.

Earn Points Across the Chase Ecosystem.

The fastest path to 125,000 points for a 5-night family trip is the Chase trifecta: Sapphire Preferred or Reserve (dining and travel), Ink Business Preferred (business spending at 3x), and Ink Business Unlimited or Cash (flat-rate earning). A family running normal spending through these cards can realistically accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually.

Don't Book Zilara When You Mean Ziva.

This sounds obvious, but adults-only Zilara properties appear in the same search results as family-friendly Ziva properties. Always confirm the property type before transferring points. Once points are transferred into Hyatt, they don't transfer back to Chase.

Points Expiration Is Activity-Based.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with a small earning or redemption every two years. A single qualifying activity — even earning 1 point through a partner — resets the clock.

Avoid Booking Refundable Rates on Points Speculatively.

Recent findings suggest that some members book award stays far out with the intent to cancel, just to "hold" dates. While Hyatt does allow cancellations, this practice can strain award availability for other members and creates unnecessary complexity. Book when you're confident.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Sources indicate that this redemption was designed — structurally, if not intentionally — for families pursuing financial independence. Here's why it fits the ChooseFI worldview so perfectly.

According to recent reports, the ideal user is a family of three to six people who want a high-quality, genuinely relaxing vacation without the mental overhead of per-meal, per-drink, per-activity budgeting. The all-inclusive format eliminates the "should we splurge on dinner?" anxiety that can undercut vacation enjoyment. You've already "paid" with points. Just enjoy.

According to recent reports, you need a minimum of 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night. For a realistic 5-night family trip, proposal for 125,000 points — or 100,000 if you hold the World of Hyatt card and qualify for the 5th night free benefit. This is very achievable if you've been accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards through normal household spending on a Sapphire card.

This redemption is also excellent for couples celebrating anniversaries or honeymoons (use Zilara for the adults-only experience), parents of young children who want a vacation where the kids are engaged so the adults can actually relax, and travelers who want a warm-weather, beach vacation without the complexity of international award flight bookings.

Sources indicate that this is NOT the right fit if you prefer boutique, off-the-beaten-path travel over resort-style vacations, you're a solo traveler (the per-person value scales poorly), or you're chasing ultra-premium redemptions like business class flights or city luxury hotels. The Hyatt portfolio has those too — but this specific sweet spot is about maximum family value, not maximum luxury status.

In a recent development, this redemption earns an **Easy** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. The ChooseFI community members who struggle with it usually hit one of two friction points, and both are easily solved. **The Earning Side: Very Easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers 1:1 to World of Hyatt instantly. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you already have access to the best transfer path. Earning 125,000 Chase UR points for a 5-night trip is a reasonable 12–18 month project for a household running normal expenses through rewards cards. **The Booking Side: Easy, With One Catch.** The Hyatt website is clean and the points booking process is straightforward. The one challenge is **peak date availability** — spring break and holiday weeks book up fast at the most popular Ziva properties. The fix is simple: use the 395-day booking window. Set a phone reminder 13 months before your target trip and search the day availability opens. **The Transfer Confidence Hurdle.** Some beginners are nervous about transferring points to Hyatt before they have a confirmed booking. The practical risk is real — if you transfer and then can't find availability, those points are stranded in Hyatt (though they're still useful for future bookings). The solution: always **confirm availability before transferring**. Hyatt lets you select dates and see the points cost before you're asked to pay. Get to that confirmation screen first, then transfer. If you can navigate a hotel booking website and move money between financial accounts, you can execute this redemption. Start with a low-stakes search on hyatt.com today — just to get comfortable with how award availability looks.

Industry observers note that check the same dates at the cash rate to calculate your cents per point value. If the cash rate is $600 per night and the award rate is 25,000 points, you are getting 2.4 cents per point. For all-inclusives, values above 2 cents per point are common and 3 or more cents per point is typical during peak season.

In a recent development, transfer the required points from your Chase account to World of Hyatt. Transfers are instant. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, you can transfer directly. Freedom and Ink Cash points can be pooled to a Sapphire card first.

According to recent reports, complete the booking using your World of Hyatt points. Select the standard room type on points — all-inclusive benefits apply to all room categories. Add any special requests for your family (crib, connecting rooms, dietary needs) in the booking notes.

If you have World of Hyatt Globalist status (earned at 60 nights or through the Globalist challenge), you unlock suite upgrades (subject to availability), late checkout, and other premium benefits. Even without elite status, the all-inclusive base experience is exceptional — every meal, drink, and activity is covered.

Industry observers note that A 7-night stay at a Hyatt Ziva or Zilara typically costs 175,000 to 245,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 to 35,000 per night depending on the property and season). This covers the room, all meals, unlimited drinks, activities, and entertainment for the duration of your stay.

At Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) properties, children typically stay and eat free when sharing a room with parents. Policies vary by property and the child's age — generally children under 12 are included at no additional cost. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only (18+). Check the specific property's policy when booking.

According to recent reports, you can, but you will get significantly less value. The Chase portal values points at 1.25 cents (CSP) or 1.5 cents (CSR) per point. Transferring to Hyatt for an all-inclusive typically delivers 2 to 4 cents per point — roughly double the portal value. For a $600-per-night all-inclusive, the portal would cost 40,000 to 48,000 Chase points per night, while a direct Hyatt transfer costs only 25,000 points.

In a recent development, most Hyatt all-inclusive award stays include resort fees in the points rate, but you may owe taxes and some incidental charges. Expect to pay $30 to $80 per night in local taxes depending on the country. Some premium experiences (spa treatments, excursions, premium alcohol) may carry additional charges. Tips for staff are at your discretion and appreciated.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Hyatt all-inclusive resorts represent the single best hotel redemption for families in the travel rewards ecosystem. The combination of a premium resort experience, all meals and drinks included, and 2 to 4 cents per point value makes this a sweet spot that is hard to beat. A family of four can enjoy a week-long beach vacation at a Hyatt Ziva for 175,000 transferable Chase points — a stay that would cost $4,000 to $7,000 in cash. For the ChooseFI community, this is the redemption that makes points tangible: your kids are splashing in the pool, you are enjoying a beachfront dinner, and the entire experience was covered by your Chase credit card rewards. Transfer to Hyatt, book early for peak dates, and give your family the vacation you have been optimizing for.

#171293. Breaking: Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3045 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Bicycling’s Gear of the Year 2027

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s no shortage of new cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable.
  • Our editors bring different perspectives to testing.
  • Our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s no shortage of new cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable. Over the past year, our editors have put those promises to the test on road and gravel rides, mountain bike trails, commutes, and in the workshop. For Gear of the Year, we’ve chosen the products that stood out most: the ones that solved a problem, made a ride more enjoyable, or delivered tangible performance that impressed us enough to recommend to you.

Our editors bring different perspectives to testing. Matt Phillips has tested bikes and gear for 30 years and has ridden more bikes than any other cycling journalist on the planet. Tara Seplavy has led product development at global bike brands, while Dan Chabanov has won national and elite titles in cyclocross and crit racing. Nearly all of us have worked in or managed bike shops.

Our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride. This year, we’ve organized them by price to make it easier to find something that fits your budget, whether you’re looking for a small upgrade or considering a bigger purchase. Whatever you choose, if it’s on this list, we think it will improve your ride.

Under $100 $100 to $300 $300 to $1,000 $1,000+.

Recent findings suggest that I get the skepticism about a product that seems to have figured out a problem that’s existed forever, but trust me, the Tyre Glider has made me completely rethink how I install tires. Instead of fighting the final few inches with my thumbs, you simply hook it under the bead and glide it around the rim. Until you use it, it just doesn’t make sense how simple and easy it is.

Industry observers note that that mechanical advantage is especially useful with tight road tires and tubeless setups, where a conventional tire lever can feel precarious with carbon rims and spokes. It won’t replace a traditional lever for every job, but for the problem it’s designed to solve, it does it really well.

Sources indicate that last summer ended with me sporting a very prominent helmet vent hole tan line on my forehead. The reason was obvious: I avoided applying sunscreen there because every formula would sweat into my eyes. This summer I set out to find one that worked.

Recent findings suggest that when I found Pelotan, I was skeptical of something marketed specifically to cyclists, but it works incredibly well. Although expensive, I found the 6-ounce bottle lasted me the entire season. It goes on light, evaporates quickly, smells nice, and most importantly doesn’t sting my eyes so I actually end up wearing it.

I often ride without gloves, so I’m picky about grips. After testing both the regular and fat versions of Ergon’s GDH Team, they’ve become my favorites for any bike built to get rowdy. The rubber is pleasantly soft and tacky, providing a secure hold with bare or gloved hands. Subtle fins under the fingers help keep my hands in place without forcing me to squeeze the bars hard.

Knipex Pliers Wrench (86 03 180).

According to recent reports, knipex makes some of the most enjoyable to use tools we have in the Bicycling workshop. The Pliers Wrench might look like an oddly shaped adjustable wrench, but its parallel jaws provide superior clamping force. It grips hardware securely without any slipping and marring.

These aren't bicycle-specific tools; they’re exceptionally good tools that happen to be incredibly useful around a bike. It comes in a range of sizes, but the 7 1/4-inch is the sweet spot: compact enough to live in a bike toolbox while still opening wide enough to handle most of the jobs I throw at it.

A front light is an easy addition to your road or gravel bike, but finding one that fits neatly on your cockpit can be tricky. Lezyne’s Road Drive 500 solves that problem with a slim, 75-gram body that tucks discreetly under a computer mount.

According to recent reports, despite its small size, the light offers a 500-lumen daytime flash and a 400-lumen mode for seeing the road or bike path after sunset. The replaceable battery lasts up to 55 hours in daytime flash mode or 4.5 hours in the 150-lumen enduro mode. Some computer mounts don’t let you adjust the beam's direction, but Lezyne includes a GoPro-style mount that lets you aim the light where you need it, at the expense of making the overall form factor a little less stealthy.

Peak Design Mobile Crossbody Multi-Strap.

Industry observers note that as a photographer and cyclist, I’m always looking for easier ways to carry cameras while riding. Peak Design’s Mobile Crossbody Multi Strap has become a useful way to keep small cameras and accessories secure and within reach.

It has been revealed that its mini quick-release mechanism lets me attach anchors to multiple devices and swap between them rapidly. I’ve used it to carry a small gimbal camera while shooting the Philly Bike Race and as an added layer of security for cameras tucked into my pockets on rides. It’s also handy when traveling, letting me keep my phone or headphones tethered while making my way through an airport.

It has been revealed that spur Cycle’s R-Pro mirror gives road and gravel riders a simple way to see what’s happening behind them. Its alloy body and glass mirror have a high-end feel that looks at home even on a pricey carbon race bike, and it installs in just a few minutes.

Recent findings suggest that I find it especially useful in heavy traffic, when a radar can be constantly pinging with notifications. A quick glance at the mirror helps me judge the distance to the vehicles behind me. It’s also handy on group rides to check that the person following me is still on my wheel. While the mirror doesn’t replace a radar, it never needs charging or pairing to a head unit.

I have found these Campagnolo 03 rotors to be categorically better than both SRAM and Shimano rotors while also being cheaper (a rare feat for a Campagnolo product).

Recent findings suggest that the main concern I have with both SRAM and Shimano’s high-end road rotors is that after hard braking, they absorb enough heat to deform and briefly make noise. Riding the same roads after switching to Campagnolo rotors? No noise after hard braking. To me, this indicates the Campagnolo rotors manage braking heat better, which gives me more confidence in their performance; plus, silence is golden. At this point, I have replaced both Shimano and SRAM rotors with these Campagnolo ones and can recommend them highly as a better rotor alternative for any road bike groupset.

Recent findings suggest that back in 2025, I bumped into an old friend at Sea Otter. He was walking around with what might be the most curious saddle prototype I’ve ever seen. It looked like it was made from plastic and Styrofoam. It was also crazy light and, according to him, fully rideable.

Now, I finally have the production version. It’s still crazy light (146g on my scale). And those funky rails? An absolute joy to use. It’s such a simple solution: the saddle slides into the clamp instead of needing to partially take everything apart in some cases. But more importantly, as someone who has always tended to sit more forward, I love the wider nose on this saddle.

In a recent development, so far I’ve enjoyed about 500 miles on this saddle, and have been very, very pleasantly surprised. It has replaced the S-Works Power Evo saddle (which is quite popular and I also found very comfortable) on my road bike, but given how the Sixpack saddle is roughly a 1/3rd of the price, just as comfortable and 25 percent lighter, I feel no need to go back to the more expensive Specialized saddle.

Vittoria Corsa Pro Control Tan, 700x42c.

It has been revealed that launched in 2025 as OEM equipment on Cervélo’s Áspero-5 gravel racer, Vittoria’s 700x42c version of its cotton-casing, all-season road tire is now available to the masses, and it’s excellent. The wider Corsa Pro Control features the cushion and grip of wider gravel rubber but rolls promptly, like a high-performance road tire. It’s the perfect upgrade for road riding on your gravel bike or building a go-fast all-road bike (provided you have enough clearance).

Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT TR.

I’ve put roughly 1,000 miles on a pair of GP5000 TT TRs (set up tubeless) without a flat. That’s not something I can say about many high-performance tires, especially ones intended only for race days. I was actually a longtime Continental skeptic, but the GP5000 S TR started to change my mind, and the TT TR convinced me to finally change my tune. It combines competitive weight and low rolling resistance with a surprisingly long lifespan. If you want a fast race tire that can also handle training miles, the TT TR is worth a look.

In a recent development, in nearly 20 years of riding and racing, I avoided the urge to get custom insoles, even though I knew early on that my feet had some weird fit concerns. This year, I finally gave in to my intrusive thoughts, and oh my god, I am not going back.

I truly didn’t think a custom insole would make as much of a difference as it did. But I’ve noticed all kinds of improvements, like my feet feeling much more stable and secure in the shoe without needing to ratchet down the closures. For the sake of experimentation, I even did a short ride with my previous comfortable (non-custom) insole setup, and I was shocked by how much discomfort I had gotten used to over the previous 20 years of riding. At this point, I would happily put custom insoles into a cheaper pair of shoes than ride stock insoles in a top-of-the-line shoe. I genuinely think the insole makes the bigger difference, and more riders should consider a pair for themselves.

Pearl Izumi Pi PRO/BLACK Mesh Jersey.

Recent findings suggest that at $190, Pearl Izumi’s Pi PRO/Black Mesh Jersey isn’t cheap, but it delivers the quality and performance I expect at that price. It’s a high-end racing jersey with understated looks, a combination that's hard to find in premium cycling kit.

The fit is cut for an aggressive position on the bike while maintaining excellent comfort and heat regulation. The paneled collar reduces pressure across the back of the neck, a common issue I’ve found with other aero-fit race jerseys. If you’re willing to pay a premium for a well-designed jersey but don’t want to look like a billboard, the Pi PRO/Black Mesh is a great option.

I am very stingy with my saddle recommendations because comfort is so uniquely personal to the rider. I know this because I ride a lot of different saddles, and I’ve discovered that only a very small minority are actually comfortable. But every so often I happen across a saddle that makes me say, “Oh, this one is special.” That’s the Ergon’s SRS Pro Carbon.

It’s plush without being squishy or saggy, offers even pressure distribution without feeling bulky, and is supportive without hot spots or pinch points. It’s also a rather good deal for a light (about 185 grams in an S/M size).

Typically, a European-made, carbon-railed saddle costs $300 or more, and that’s before you get into 3D-printed tops, so $220 seems almost reasonable.

I use a torque wrench almost every time I work on my bikes. Tightening parts to the correct torque helps prevent component failures, especially with carbon components, lightweight parts, or suspension linkages. Of the several torque wrenches in Bicycling’s workshop, I most often reach for Topeak’s Torq Stick Pro Digital.

The wrench adjusts from 1 to 20 Nm in one-tenth Nm increments. It beeps as you approach your selected torque and buzzes when you reach it. While it costs more than an analog wrench, I find it to be more precise and much easier to use, especially on parts that have torque ratings that include decimal points. Topeak’s set also includes common metric hex and Torx bits, an extender, an 8mm crowfoot for brake bleeds, and a small ratchet driver.

It has been revealed that heat training is a tool many of the world’s best bike racers use to prepare for hot summer races. The Core 2 Heat Sensor makes it easier to track and monitor that process, but I’ve found it useful even without fully optimizing my heat training.

Sources indicate that the sensor monitors skin and core temperature and combines that information with heart-rate data to give you a heat-strain index. That makes it easier to gauge how your body is responding to the heat while riding. I use the sensor all summer to watch for spikes in my body temperature and take preventive measures before I overheat. With more summer events likely happening during periods of high heat, monitoring your body temperature more closely can be not just helpful, but tangibly beneficial.

Q36.5 Dottore Pro Long Sleeve Jersey.

The Q36.5 Dottore Pro jersey works across a wider range of temperatures than any other long-sleeve jersey I’ve tried. It holds enough heat to keep me comfortable on cool rides, but it also pulls moisture away from my body and feels cool enough for warmer days.

I’ve used it as a layer on a soaking-wet 50-degree ride, worn it on a 75-degree summer day, and ridden in it in plenty of conditions in between. On some of those rides, there were other pieces of clothing I would have changed, but I would have picked the same jersey every time. Its versatility means it can replace multiple layers, making it well worth the asking price.

The Varia RearVue 820 is Garmin’s first full upgrade to its successful radar light in nearly six years. It delivers more information to compatible Garmin Edge head units, offers brighter light, supports USB-C charging, provides longer battery life, and extends detection range. On the road, the RearVue 820 feels like a noticeable step up from other radar units—notably, it consistently detects vehicles approaching from behind earlier than other devices.

In a recent development, same-speed tracking was another revelation. Not having to constantly check whether the car that dropped off my screen was still following me or had turned into a driveway is something no other radar unit does reliably, and it's a big reason I would choose the 820 over other units. If you’re using a modern Garmin cycling computer that supports advanced tracking features, the Garmin Varia RearVue 820 is more than just an patch to the RTL 515. It’s a big step forward in cycling radar technology.

In a recent development, but even if you’re not using the latest Edge device, my comparative testing highlighted the 820 was always the first radar to detect an approaching car, sometimes by several seconds. Sure, things like better battery life, a more convenient charging standard, and a brighter light are great. But when it comes to cycling radars, better, faster detection is king, and right now the RearVue 820 wears that crown.

The Apex Aeon bibs are stupid expensive, but great bibs are one of the few pieces of cycling equipment worth splurging on. These have become my favorite pair for long, hard, hot rides, maintaining their support and comfort from start to finish.

The straps and lowers are thick and feel almost overbuilt, a welcome change from cycling apparel that can feel wispy and fragile. The chamois is medium-thick and the firmest I can remember using, but it’s fantastically comfortable without feeling like a diaper. Like the rest of the bib, it shines brightest on longer rides. I’ve worn almost nothing else this summer, and whenever I ride in a different pair, I invariably wish I’d grabbed these instead.

Industry observers note that it is no understatement to say SRAM is on a roll. Thanks to a combination of performance, features, and impeccable timing, its drivetrains are the benchmarks for mountain, gravel, and road riding at the moment. On the road, the newest Red (E1) stormed into the market with superbly comfortable hoods, brilliant brakes, and excellent shifting. One would be wise never to count Shimano out, but Red E1 declared to the world that it had forever altered the drivetrain status quo.

Industry observers note that other Bicycling editors and I have long argued that top-of-the-line drivetrains, especially in the electronic era, are never the smart buy. Give up a bit of weight, and you can get all the performance of a brand’s top-tier group for a lot less money. And that’s the case with SRAM’s Rival E1. It offers all the performance and improvements of Red E1, along with SRAM’s impressive ecosystem interoperability. The bonus buttons on the hoods are the only feature you might miss: Red and Force have them; Rival does not. Aside from those, Rival E1 offers the benchmark performance of Red E1 without the painful hit to the wallet.

In any given year, I ride between 20 and 30 different bikes (usually with a variety of wheels), and I will also likely test anywhere between five and ten standalone wheelsets. That is, I ride a lot of different road wheels every year, and these Rovals earned my Gear of the Year endorsement because I keep coming back to them.

In a recent development, one of the things I like most: I think Specialized has cracked the secret sauce with their carbon spokes. Every other carbon-spoked wheel I have tried has a much harsher ride than a traditional steel-spoke wheel. Both the Rapide Sprint and the Rapide CLX III feel more like traditional wheels, just with a bunch of weight lopped off. I keep coming back to the deeper Sprint version over the more all-around CLX III because I don’t really feel the roughly 90g difference, but I definitely notice the extra speed on flat and rolling terrain. It’s pretty wild that Specialized has managed to make a set of 60-ish mm deep wheels (63 mm and 58 mm deep, to be exact) this light while also making them feel so smooth.

#171292. A Runner Took a Midrace Puff of Weed at the NYC Marathon. Now, She’s Disqualified.

A Runner Took a Midrace Puff of Weed at the NYC Marathon. Now, She’s Disqualified.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral.
  • "Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.
  • Industry observers note that the Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.

"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.

Industry observers note that the Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and New York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.

Recent findings suggest that as far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.

In a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and said she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.

"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the Upcoming York Post.

Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.

Recent findings suggest that she'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in New York, too. One prerace Instagram video joked about giving up dating apps in favor of training for a marathon, while her bright pink marathon shirt doubled as a personal advertisement. The front read, "Andrea, 35, Single. Great Credit. Bad Judgment," while the back added, "Looking for a man with more endurance than my ex.".

It has been revealed that her latest social media introduction has since acquired another word: "35. Single. Great credit. Poor judgment. Disqualified.".

Sager still has her finisher medal, and the extra attention has brought some unexpected opportunities.

"I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.

Sources indicate that sager mentioned she was told she can participate in future NYRR events, despite the removal of her November 1 result. Runner's World contacted the organization for comment and confirmation of her eligibility but received no response.

As for racing looks, Sager said she has HYROX Houston on her calendar for April 2027. And someone in her Instagram comments has suggested a shirt idea for her next event:.

"I smoked weed at the NYC marathon and all I got was a DQ.".

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

Latest Update: 6 Core-Strengthening Exercises to Spice Up Your Routine

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics.
  • Research indicates just how key core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine.
  • Recent findings suggest that the authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics. But your torso muscles—which include your abs, back, glutes, and hip flexors—play a crucial role in cycling that goes way beyond looks.

Research indicates just how key core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine. One 2019 study, published in PLoS One, found that an eight-week core training program improved balance and core endurance (which you need to maintain posture through long miles) in the 21 college athletes who participated. Another research review, published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2022, says core training should have a place in all athletes’ training programs.

Recent findings suggest that the authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability. The authors also write that these core strength benefits help prevent “energy leaks,” therefore leading to better performance.

Industry observers note that to help you gain these benefits of a strong midsection, you need a solid workout to add to your routine. Thankfully, Noam Tamir, C.S.C.S., founder and CEO of TS Fitness in New York City, created this dumbbell core-strengthening workout.

Sources indicate that in addition to the research that proves the benefits of core strength for athletes, the moves Tamir chose for this workout make an ideal mix for those looking to improve performance. Not only will the moves improve your stability in an upright posture, allowing you to ride and breathe more efficiently, but they also target the core from multiple angles, hitting every muscle of the torso.

Sources indicate that even better: While these moves resemble familiar core exercises, each one has a creative spin. This means they not only challenge your body in fun new ways, but also engage your brain.

How to use this list: Do each exercise below, in order, for the reps listed. Repeat for 3-4 rounds. Rest as needed between exercises and rounds.

Sources indicate that tamir demonstrates the exercises in the video above so you can learn proper form. You will need one light to medium dumbbell for this workout. An exercise mat is optional.

Why it works: The half-kneeling halo exercise focuses on trunk stability. “It works the core at 360 degrees because the dumbbell is moving around the body while you’re maintaining an upright position,” Tamir says. You do the same thing on a ride—hold a strong posture and upright body position while your arms and legs move.

How to do it: Start kneeling, right knee on ground, and left foot planted in front, both knees bent 90 degrees. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chin. Keeping torso and lower body steady, circle dumbbell clockwise around head. Elbows stay close to head. Return to chin. Repeat in other direction. Do 8-10 reps in each direction. Switch leg stance each round.

Recent findings suggest that why it works: Target the obliques with this rotational move. You’ll also hit the rectus abdominis (those six-pack looking abs) and work on coordination of the upper and lower body, Tamir explains.

How to do it: Start seated on floor. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chest. Lean back slightly, and lift legs off floor, hips and knees bent about 45 degrees. Bring dumbbell to outside of left hip by rotating torso to right and extend left leg straight out, foot lowering close to floor. Keep shoulders down and back. Next, bend left knee and extend right leg out, lowering foot close to floor and lift dumbbell up and over to the right, rotating torso to the right. Bring weight back down to outside of left hip, as you extend right leg out and pull left knee back in. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Sources indicate that why it works: This explosive movement focuses on the hips. “The core is not limited to just the abdominal muscles,” Tamir says. “You also need the whole body to create power, strength, and endurance.” This exercise gets more muscles in on the action, while the hinge motion helps to improve riding, especially during acceleration, he adds.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbell in right hand down by side. Hinge at hips, by sending butt straight back, dumbbell reaching behind you. Keep back flat and core engaged. Using glutes, drive feet into floor and extend hips. Let the power of your glutes send dumbbell forward and up to shoulder height. Engage core, like you’re hitting a standing plank position at the top. Let the momentum of the dumbbell guide you back into a hinge position. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps.

Why it works: This anti-rotation exercise works the deep core muscles, including the transverse abdominis that wraps around your midsection, and the multifidus, the posterior core muscles that protect your spine, Tamir explains. “It also helps to stabilize the pelvis to reduce risk of injury,” he adds, and aids in strong posture by working the back.

How to do it: Start in a plank position, left hand on a dumbbell, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be slightly wider than hips. Pull left elbow straight up, dumbbell reaching to ribcage. Lower back down. Repeat. Keep hips as steady as possible. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: The pullover crunch focuses mainly on the rectus abdominus (the muscles on the front of the torso) which helps to stabilize the spine and, in turn, maintain good form, Tamir claims.

According to recent reports, how to do it: Lie faceup, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands overhead, dumbbell behind you, arms extended. Bend knees, feet planted on floor. Pull dumbbell overhead and crunch up, lifting head, neck, and shoulders off floor. At the same time, lift feet off floor, driving knees toward arms. Slowly lower back down, dumbbell hovering off floor behind you, and feet hovering off floor in front of you. Repeat. Do 12-15 reps.

In a recent development, why it works: This is a great move for stabilizing the spine, while teaching abdominal bracing, Tamir states. The weight on one side also forces the core to resist rotation, which you need for efficiency on the road.

In a recent development, how to do it: Lie face up. Hold dumbbell in right hand over shoulder, arm straight. Extend left arm overhead, biceps by ear. Lift head, neck, shoulders, and legs a few inches off floor. Use legs to rock back and floor, maintaining the hollow body position. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat with dumbbell in left hand.

Latest Update: Procrastinating Your Winter Runs? Here’s What Will Actually Get You Out the Door, According to a Sports Psychologist

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Recent findings suggest that nine months of the year, I rarely struggle to get myself out the door for a run.
  • In a recent development, while this does have occasional productivity benefits—my kitchen floor shines and my email inbox stays at zero—I’ll find myself more than an hour later no closer to starting my run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that nine months of the year, I rarely struggle to get myself out the door for a run. Then winter arrives, the temperatures drop, and suddenly it’s three straight months of daily prerun procrastination: I look for any excuse, task, or chore to delay heading out into the cold or stepping on the treadmill.

In a recent development, while this does have occasional productivity benefits—my kitchen floor shines and my email inbox stays at zero—I’ll find myself more than an hour later no closer to starting my run. Except by then, I’m crunched for time, it’s pitch-black outside, and the whole process has drained enough of my mental energy that I’d rather push those miles to tomorrow.

In a recent development, I know I’m not alone: Even professional marathoners fall into the “run-crastination” spiral. Previously, Des Linden and Kara Goucher discussed their own experiences on their podcast, Nobody Asked Us with Des & Kara. Still, I’d much rather find a way to avoid getting sucked in so I can get on with my run and my day, and enjoy both a little more as a result.

So, I asked a sports psychologist what actually works to get you out the door in the winter when anything sounds better than a run—plus when it’s actually a better idea to skip the miles.

Recent findings suggest that the first step to beating prerun procrastination? Determine the reason you’re doing it. “Procrastination is usually one of two things,” Justin Ross, Psy.D., a clinical sports psychologist and UESCA-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World. “One: It’s an avoidance strategy, because what you’re about to do is uncomfortable, unpleasant, hard, or challenging. But, it can also signal toward a different need that’s not being met.”.

In the winter months—especially for driven runners coming off a fall marathon season—that other need can be rest. “True athletic wisdom is knowing the difference between when procrastination is avoidance, and when it’s a sign that you need something other than a run that day,” Ross explains.

Gaining that wisdom as an athlete takes time, practice, and some trial and error. The best way to start? Focus on creating “systems” that make procrastination less likely so you can more easily identify the action that aligns with your needs, goals, and values, Ross notes. Most times, these systems (which we outline below) lead to better outcomes than trying to rely on willpower alone or following an impulse in the moment.

Industry observers note that if you find yourself avoiding a run, remove as many obstacles as possible that stand between you and getting out the door or to the gym. For Ross, that means setting out all his running clothes and fuel ahead of time so he doesn’t need to hunt for that one pair of gloves he hasn’t seen since last January.

“Without preparation, procrastination becomes a whole lot easier because you have all these extra hurdles,” he explains. “When it’s dark and cold in the winter, you need to problem-solve in ways that you don’t need to when it’s beautiful out and you’re excited to run.”.

It has been revealed that for me, that means making sure my headlamp actually has working batteries if I’m planning to run outside in the evenings. If I’m hitting the treadmill, I cue up a playlist, TV show, or podcast on my phone and stock my gym bag with a postrun snack and a full water bottle.

When you’re procrastinating a run, try shifting your focus from what you’re doing to why you’re doing it. “Remind yourself why this run is important to you or how it helps you,” Ross says. For example, you might think about your values or current goals and consider how this workout brings you closer to them.

Industry observers note that I’ve found I’m motivated simply by the fact that running makes me feel like my favorite version of myself—and that boosts my mood more than any race-specific or fitness goal. But you might be more excited by the idea that staying consistent with your training over the winter will set you up for a stronger chance at a marathon PR in the spring.

Consider what might add a little bit more spark to your routine or make it more enticing. You might decide to meet up with a friend or local run club for a few miles. You might look forward to your treadmill run as “the 30 minutes of my day where I don’t have to be bothered and I can just watch my favorite show [alone],” says Ross.

The reward mindset helps you refocus on what brings you joy, instead of just relieving the pressure of needing to get in a workout.

Recent findings suggest that another helpful strategy? Doing the absolute bare minimum. “Runners often fall into this trap of having rigid rules around their exercise or their training,” says Ross. Try letting go of whatever mileage or workout you had planned for the day, and tell yourself that you’ll just run for 10 minutes and then reassess how you feel.

You may even want to adjust your whole training standard ahead of the winter season, Ross claims. For example, you might reduce the length, intensity, or frequency of the workouts you initiative to do each week. Or, instead of targeting a specific pace or mileage requirement, run or cross-train solely based on time. “Think about being more flexible in your approach during the winter months. Maybe you aim for the minimal effective dose to get the benefit you’re looking for, like just running for 20 minutes if your usual standard is 60,” Ross suggests.

Ross explains that winter can be a meaningful time for runners to examine what rules they have around their training that might be adding pressure. For example, I used to follow a silly rule from an old college teammate who said that any run shorter than three miles “didn’t count” as a true run. Once I finally let go of that, I found it much easier to get moving—even if it was just for an easy walk in the park near my house.

“This time of year, see how you can approach exercise from an overall health or mood-boost perspective instead of a training perspective,” suggests Ross.

Also, question any rigid rules you’ve established for yourself around volume, pace, or mileage—like making sure to hit a specific number of miles every week or setting a minimum pace requirement for all your runs—because they may backfire and lead to mental burnout over the long term, he notes.

Sources indicate that if you’ve done all the above and you still can’t get yourself out the door, a run may not actually be what you need. “If you keep hitting the moment to head out and that intuitive voice says, ‘I just really don’t want to,’ try listening to that voice. Listen to your body,” Ross suggests. “It’s okay to give yourself permission for rest and recovery—especially during this time of year.”.

She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

Fashion Has Entered Its Running Era

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
