In a recent development, getting faster isn’t just about training harder. It also requires smarter recovery.

While there’s plenty of advice about the importance of rest days and how slowly you should go during easy recovery runs, there’s considerably less discussion about exactly how long those runs should last.

Significant picture, recovery runs should help you stay consistent between harder sessions; they shouldn’t leave you carrying extra fatigue into your next workout. However, simply running at an easy pace doesn’t guarantee an easy training load because the longer you run, the more energy you use and the more repetitive impact you take on.

So how long should your recovery runs last to maintain the volume-building, bloodflow-boosting benefits? And what signs mean it’s time to cut the run short?

We asked run coaches and exercise physiologists to explain how to find the right recovery run duration to ensure you’re not dragging for your next workout and when calling it a (rest) day might work best.

Recovery runs allow runners to increase their overall aerobic training volume without taking a complete rest day after every hard session, claims run coach, author, and founder of 80/20 Endurance, Matt Fitzgerald. For instance, if the sole objective were to recover from quality runs as rapidly as possible, total rest (a.k.a. not running at all) is more effective.

But receiving the benefits of recovery runs without elevating fatigue or injury risk depends on keeping duration within a certain range.

Recent findings suggest that “As a run extends, we’re also continuing to consume energy and introduce mechanical load,” explains Pamela Geisel, CSCS, RRCA-certified run coach, exercise physiologist, and director of Performance and Wellness Services at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York City. In other words, your muscles are still contracting, your body is still using fuel, and your bones, tendons, and joints are absorbing the repetitive impact of every stride.

If you extend a recovery run too long, the stress caused by this additional workload begins to outweigh the aerobic benefits of the run and can lead to the aforementioned heightened fatigue and injury risk, especially if you’re recovering from a particularly demanding training session.

In a recent development, this logic is exactly why experts all agree that recovery runs absolutely can go on for too long. The tricky part is finding the line.

“There’s no established duration or mileage at which an easy run becomes detrimental to recovery,” claims Michael Landram, an exercise physiologist and assistant professor at the University of Scranton.

Instead, each person’s ideal duration depends on a variety of factors, including training history, current fatigue, nutrition, sleep, and the demands of any upcoming workouts, Landram explains.

Here’s a three-step checklist for making sure yours fall in the right range.

Usually, Geisel recommends keeping recovery runs between 20 and 40 minutes in length, but that window should shift depending on how much you’re accustomed to running.

It has been revealed that for example, if you’re averaging around 20 miles per week, Geisel suggests aiming for approximately 15 to 25 minutes. If you’re regularly logging up to 60 miles per week, you can pencil in 25- to 45-minute recovery sessions.

And remember, these recommendations are starting points, not strict limits. Danny Mackey, head coach of the Brooks Beasts Track Club, says he might prescribe a recovery run of just 20 minutes for an 800-meter specialist, while long-distance runners accustomed to running 75 to 80 miles per week can comfortably handle a 60-minute recovery run.

Additionally, it’s vital to take into consideration how long you’ve maintained your current weekly mileage.

According to recent reports, landram explains that a runner who’s consistently logged 50-mile weeks for several years may tolerate longer recovery runs than someone who’s only recently built up to that level. Even if both runners in this example have similar cardiovascular fitness, their muscles may not be equally adapted to the repetitive demands of 50-mile weeks.

So, if you’ve recently increased your weekly mileage, stick to shorter recovery runs and gradually extend their duration as your body adjusts.

Industry observers note that if you’re relatively new to running, are only running a few days per week, or have only easy runs on your schedule as you build endurance and consistency, you may not need a dedicated recovery run at all. Rest days allow for proper rejuvenation between workouts.

Sources indicate that fitzgerald recommends using your typical easy-run duration as a reference point and making recovery runs shorter and slower (zone 1, anyone?). If your scheduled easy runs are usually 60 minutes long, for instance, a recovery run—particularly one scheduled after hard, quality workouts—might last 40 minutes or less, at an even lower intensity.

It has been revealed that if you’ve just completed a particularly demanding interval session, long run, or race, consider keeping your recovery run at the shorter end of your usual range. The same applies if you have another hard workout scheduled within the next 24 to 48 hours.

Heat, hills, and uneven terrain can also make an otherwise easy session more taxing, so it’s worth considering an even shorter duration in those circumstances.

Overall, your recovery-run duration should reflect what your body is accustomed to handling, rather than a mileage target you’re trying to reach.

Even if you’ve planned your recovery run carefully, it’s important to pay attention to how your body responds once you start moving.

Recent findings suggest that one of the first warning signs is a change in perceived exertion. If your usual recovery pace suddenly feels harder than it should or your legs feel unusually heavy, you may need to reconsider how long you’re running.

Geisel also recommends paying attention to changes in your stride, including heavier foot strikes and other form problems getting worse as the run progresses.

Sources indicate that the metrics available on your watch can also indicate a recovery run has gone too long. For example, an unusually elevated heart rate at your normal easy pace may signal you’re carrying too much fatigue, Landram explains. Though remember heat, dehydration, sleep, and stress can also affect heart rate, so pair it with how you feel to determine if you’re going too long.

If you’re feeling unusually tired during a recovery run, Shannon Hugard, a biomechanics researcher at the University of Oregon, recommends a simple midrun check-in. “If you’re feeling more fatigued or sore than usual, run that first mile,” she advises. “See how you’re feeling. If you’re still sore or fatigued, cut that easy run duration by about 25 to 50 percent.” If you’re experiencing pain that affects your stride, however, it’s better to stop immediately rather than push through.

It’s also worth paying attention to how you feel after your recovery run.

Industry observers note that for Mackey, the biggest giveaway that an athlete isn’t recovering adequately is often what happens during their next hard workout. “If they’re struggling to hit their usual paces, feeling unusually fatigued, or showing a noticeable drop in motivation, I know it’s time to reassess their recovery sessions,” he claims.

Sources indicate that if these warning signs persist, the best option might just be skipping your next recovery run altogether. A rest day, walk, or low-impact cross-training session can give your body a break from the repetitive loading of running, particularly when you’re dealing with lingering fatigue.

Industry observers note that and if you think cutting a run short feels like a missed training opportunity, take a cue from the pros: “This is one of the biggest differences I see in elite runners,” claims Fitzgerald. “They take pride in their restraint and ability to hold back, because they know it’s part of a more intentional strategy.”.

Industry News: Research Reveals This Is the Best Way to Balance Strength Training and Running

💡 Key Takeaways

  • But sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles.
  • So if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, there’s a reason why run coaches and personal trainers emphasize strength training in addition to running: Practicing both forms of exercise will allow you to build stronger muscles and increase your aerobic capacity at the same time. Combining strength training and a running schedule means you boost your fitness in multiple ways.

But sometimes, especially after a heavy leg day workout, your body can feel pretty tired and sore and seemingly not ready to take on miles. This isn’t just in your head. According to a review of 132 studies, it takes a full day or two more to recover from resistance training than it does a high-intensity run.

So if you’ve ever been tempted to skip the weights today in favor of a better run tomorrow, consider the advantages of strength training. Not only does it just feel good to move your muscles through full ranges of motion, especially after sitting all day, but it can also pay off in the long run for your run performance and overall health. In fact, several studies point to better running economy, as well as VO2 max and anaerobic threshold, when following a program that incorporates both endurance training and strength training.

According to recent reports, instead of ditching strength exercises to focus on mileage, the key is creating a strength training schedule that optimally fits into your run training. After all, strength training is supposed to help, not harm, your running. Here’s how to achieve that.

Get the strength initiative that works for all runners! Race-Ready Strength, our upcoming progressive 4-week training program, will get you in the best shape to reach your racing goals.

To get it right, you need to understand how your body reacts to moving heavy stuff. Picture pushing a hand truck 50 feet. Pretty easy. That’s running—your body is the hand truck and it moves its own weight rather effortlessly. Now slide the hand truck under a fridge and push it just five feet. A lot more difficult. That’s mechanical loading; it’s why 10 heavy squats feels so much more challenging than 1,000 foot strikes.

The reason strength training makes you faster is because it lowers the amount of energy required to hit a certain pace, explains Kenji Doma, Ph.D., a sports and exercise scientist at James Cook University in Queensland, Australia, and author of a 2014 study on strength training and running performance published in the European Journal of Sports Science.

Doma has also studied the effects of combining aerobic exercise and strength training on muscle hypertrophy and strength, as published in a Sports Medicine systematic review and meta-analysis in 2022. The researchers found that combining the two types of training doesn’t hinder strength and muscle-building gains, but can compromise explosive strength gains when performed in the same session—something to consider if that’s your goal.

Sources indicate that what’s important to note is that when you lift weights, your brain alters its neural recruitment pattern, calling up the most fatigue-resistant muscle fibers so you exert less energy. That’s why you don’t want to skimp on strength training. Doma’s research offers guidance on how best to combine mile repeats and repetitions in the gym for a more well-rounded running and strength training schedule.

According to recent reports, in the study that focused specifically on running performance, 15 runners of a wide range of ability and average weekly mileage did different strength-training sessions on three occasions. One workout was a high-intensity, total-body session, one was high intensity but for legs only, and one was a low-intensity, total-body workout.

Six hours after each workout, the runners did a treadmill test for 10 minutes at 70 percent of ventilatory threshold pace (easy), then 10 minutes at 90 percent of threshold pace (roughly close to half marathon pace), and then as long as possible at 110 percent of threshold pace. The runners also did the treadmill test at the outset of the study, to get a benchmark for how they would perform when fresh.

The high-intensity strength workouts significantly lessened the runners’ time to exhaustion at the end of the treadmill test. In the benchmark test, they’d lasted an average of close to five minutes at 110 percent of threshold pace. After each of the high-intensity strength sessions, time to exhaustion was almost a minute less, suggesting that the hard weight workouts six hours earlier had dramatically decreased the runners’ ability to sustain fast running.

Doma states his findings have practical implications for how runners should arrange their workouts.

First, he advises not to schedule a hard running workout later in the day of a weight session. “Running at maximal effort is impaired six hours [after] lower-extremity resistance training, and therefore trained to moderately-trained runners will need more than that to recover for running sessions set at high intensities,” he says.

Sources indicate that plus, running at maximal effort is still impaired 24 hours after lower-extremity resistance training, according to Doma. “Therefore, in the case of trained and moderately-trained runners undertaking high-intensity running sessions after lower-extremity resistance training, they may need more than one day to recover.”.

Doma also found that running performance at lower intensities was unaffected by the weight workouts. “Runners could undertake strength training and running sessions on the same day six hours apart as long as the running session is set at submaximal intensities,” Doma indicates. In other words, if you have an easy, long run, or recovery run on the schedule, it’ll be fine to double up that day, as long as workouts are more than six hours apart.

It has been revealed that if possible, Doma suggests arranging your schedule so that on days that you run and lift, running comes first. “I found that lower-extremity resistance training performed six hours prior to running sessions at moderate to high intensities cause carryover effects of fatigue the next day to a greater extent than the reverse sequence,” he indicates. “Therefore, if undertaking lower-extremity resistance training and running sessions on the same day, it is best to undertake a running session before a strength training session. For example, running in the morning before work and lower-extremity resistance training in the evening after work.”.

According to recent reports, in this scenario, it would make sense to have that morning run be one of your harder workouts of the week. Your workout the following day would then be an easy recovery run, which would be warranted even without the evening lifting, but is that much more called for on the basis of Doma’s research.

This sequence would also mesh with many coaches’ recommendation to have great discrepancy between your hard and easy days, so that you can better recover from your toughest workouts—instead of including hard elements of non-running training on your easy running days.

Scott is a veteran running, fitness, and health journalist who has held senior editorial positions at Runner’s World and Running Times. Much of his writing translates sport science research and elite best practices into practical guidance for everyday athletes. He is the author or coauthor of several running books, including Running Is My Therapy, Advanced Marathoning, and Meb for Mortals. Scott has also written about running for Slate, The Atlantic, the Washington Post, and other members of the sedentary media. His lifetime running odometer is past 110,000 miles, but he’s as much in love as ever.

The Companion Pass is valid for the remainder of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the entire following calendar year. If you earn it on January 2nd, you get nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it in November, you get roughly 14 months. This is why timing your earning to January is the critical optimization.

Sources indicate that yes. Signup bonuses, spending on Southwest cards, points transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, and points earned through the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal all count as qualifying points. The only points that do not count are those purchased directly from Southwest.

Yes. The Companion Pass works on both cash-purchased flights and flights booked with Rapid Rewards points. Your companion pays only taxes — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights — regardless of how you booked the ticket.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Southwest Companion Pass is the single most powerful domestic travel rewards benefit available to FI-minded families and couples. At a cost of 135,000 qualifying points — achievable through credit card signup bonuses and Chase transfers — you unlock nearly two full years of 2-for-1 flights on every Southwest route with no blackout dates and no change fees. A family of four taking six domestic trips per year can realistically save $2,000 to $4,000 annually, money that goes straight back into your investment accounts. Time your earning to January, stack your signup bonuses, and designate your most frequent travel partner. This is the redemption that makes domestic travel a rounding error in your FI budget.

Best GPS Bike Computers of 2026: 10 Editor-Tested Picks for Navigation, Training Data, and Battery Life

📅 25 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Bike computers are one of the best equipment upgrades you can make for your road, gravel, and mountain bike rides.
  • I use a cycling computer on virtually every ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Bike computers are one of the best equipment upgrades you can make for your road, gravel, and mountain bike rides. Head units display common metrics like speed, distance, and power, and track and record your data, so you can download it and crunch the info after your rides. They’re also great for ride navigation and following pre-planned routes. Today’s leading head units put features from turn-by-turn GPS navigation to real-time performance analytics at your fingertips.

I use a cycling computer on virtually every ride. I do this to test more devices and log the many miles I pedal on different bikes and equipment. An upside of always riding with a GPS-equipped computer is mid-ride exploration and changing rides on the fly. Now, if I’m curious about a road or potential shortcut, I can check whether it goes where I think. And rerouting features on many computers let me cut rides short and head home if weather changes.

Many latest bike computers integrate with popular platforms such as Strava, Trailforks, and Garmin Connect. Our favorite models offer real-time hill profiles on climbs and feature data-rich maps for precise navigation, even when descending switchback roads at speed. Some models even feature solar charging and real-time weather alerts. But beyond the fancy features, every bike computer does the same basic job—record your ride and display the data you need.

Since our editors and test team use cycling computers on nearly every ride, we’re constantly riding the newest models. Brands offer dozens of cycling-specific computers, and many have similar shapes, screens, and button layouts. However, as our testing has proven, the differences are in the details. And picking the right cycling computer for your needs makes rides much more enjoyable.

According to recent reports, buying Advice: Modern cycling computers operate a lot like cell phones (the Hammerhead is actually an Android-based platform). So, think of their operating systems like using a mobile device. What works for someone else might not be right for you, but that doesn’t make it a bad computer. Try computers before buying (if possible), because you cannot change the interface without getting a upcoming device.

The Wahoo Elemnt Bolt V3 combines excellent features at a great price, making it a strong option for a wide range of cyclists. In his review of the Bolt V3, Test Editor Dan Chabanov dug into the revamped computer’s details. Its features include a 2.3-inch high-resolution display with 16 million colors for increased clarity and improved battery life (up to 20 hours). The Bolt’s interface still prioritizes information in an easy-to-read format and uses buttons rather than a touch screen.

Sources indicate that the Bolt displays grade and climb profiles that show difficulty by assigning different background colors depending on the hill’s gradient (red being the steepest). This makes it easy to see at a glance what the climb ahead of you will be like.

Sources indicate that wahoo computers feature an easy setup process and an intuitive companion app that connects to third-party tools. The Bolt V3 has 32 GB of onboard storage, which is enough to store maps for the United States and thousands of routes. The Elemnt Bolt V3 gives you everything you need (and nothing you don’t).

In a recent development, garmin introduced the all-new Edge 850 late last year. It features a slightly larger and brighter screen, an integrated bell, voice prompts, and more. However, it also adds $150 to the price. For this reason, we’re still substantial fans of Garmin’s Edge 840.

While the Edge 840 features less functionality than the newer Edge 850, it costs significantly less and has a longer battery life. The 840 provides riders with all the data they need to manage a training program and track progress. These include VO2 max output (when paired with a heart monitor), recovery time, training load, and heat and altitude acclimation. It also offers cycling dynamics like position, right/left balance (when paired with a power meter), and bike setup. The Edge 840 provides plenty of detailed info if you like charts and analyzing data.

In a recent development, overall, the 840 is an excellent option for riders who love training and digging into data. It offers a reasonable balance of price and features in the generally pricey Garmin bike computer lineup. If you need more battery life, choose the 840 Solar, which extends usage up to an impressive 32 hours.

Industry observers note that if you want the maximum possible battery life for a cycling computer, Coros’ recently launched Dura 2 is your standout choice. Although the upcoming Dura costs double the original, the Dura 2 features a sleeker design, improved maps and navigation, and clean pairing with devices such as power meters, heart rate monitors, and electronic drivetrains.

Like the original Dura, the second-gen model gets exceptional battery life, and that’s without considering its solar charging capabilities. Coros claims the Dura 2 achieves up to 120 hours of use on a single charge. In Dan Chabanov’s testing, he still had 77 percent battery remaining after 30 hours of ride time—that’s frankly exceptional for a cycling computer.

However, with its great battery life and solar charging come a couple of downsides. Notably, the price: the Dura 2 costs $499 compared to the original model’s $250 price tag. The other notable miss is the Dura 2’s rerouting. It requires a connection to Coros’ smartphone app, and we found it hit-or-miss in our testing.

If you don’t have the budget for a Wahoo, Garmin, or Hammerhead computer, you still have a few solid options. For only $100, Magene offers a full-color touchscreen, turn-by-turn navigation, and even has a hill gradient feature and Strava segment integration (with a firmware enhancement). That puts the mighty little C506 in the league of its major-name competitors at a fraction of the price.

Industry observers note that the low price, however, means the C506 isn’t quite as polished as the pricey head units. For example, you must pair your smartphone to upload routes. Some owners also report touchscreen lag and software bugs. However, to its credit, Magene’s firmware upgrades have added a lot of functionality and improved shortcomings. If you have a limited budget and don’t mind a few usage quirks, the C506’s price and low weight make it hard to pass up.

Industry observers note that since launching two and a half years ago, Hammerhead’s Karoo computer has consistently remained my go-to head unit for road and gravel rides. Why? Because it’s the right size, has excellent navigation, pairs well with SRAM components, and features my favorite user interface.

In a recent development, the Karoo’s navigation and touchscreen are best-in-class. On-the-fly route planning is easy—I love its ability to navigate to any Google Maps destination (shared via the Hammerhead app) and use the feature often. The Karoo’s UI is very intuitive, and it’s easy to find functions or customize the screens (compared to the bloated interfaces on some competitors’ cycling computers).

While the Karoo doesn’t look much different from its predecessor, the Karoo 2 (yes, it’s called the Karoo even though it’s the third-gen), it offers many solid updates: A dedicated power button, improved battery life (up to 35 hours), an ambient light sensor, and automatic backlight control.

Hammerhead’s smartphone app offers automatic ride uploads and live tracking—you can send a link to family or friends to track your ride progress. Another Hammerhead strong suit is its bi-weekly software updates that remedy bugs and add useful features. Combined with the ability to sideload third-party apps, the Karoo’s function constantly improves.

For AXS-equipped bike owners, the Karoo integrates tightly with SRAM’s electronic components. For example, you can program AXS shift buttons (including the bonus buttons on Force and Red hoods) directly from the computer. Read more about this integration in Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips’ story “SRAM Releases its New Red AXS Road Group.”.

If you only need a cycling computer for the basics (speed, distance, heart rate, power, etc.) and don’t want a cellphone-sized device hanging off your bar, the Cycplus M2 is a great option. This tiny computer covers all the bases at a fraction of the cost of massive-name competitors. It also has great styling that won’t look out of place on lightweight bikes, and it's small enough to use on the trail.

Recent findings suggest that while the M2 lacks amenities such as a touchscreen display or mapping, it features a 70-hour battery life, GPS tracking, and ANT+ and Bluetooth connectivity to your power meter and HRM. Cycplus’s app will also sync your rides to Strava to track your progress.

Overhauled in 2025, Wahoo’s Elemnt Roam is consistently one of our favorite cycling computers. Updates to the Roam V3 over the V2 include a larger touchscreen display, dual-band GPS for enhanced connection in mountains and dense woods, 64GB internal storage, and improved battery life.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to the V3’s larger size and weight, Wahoo added a speaker for voice navigation and an integrated bell (activated with a quick two-finger tap on the screen). However, Wahoo removed the V2’s fan-favorite LED status lights. Additionally, we found the screen brightness a bit dim in our testing compared to Garmin and Hammerhead displays.

As Chabanov noted in his detailed review of the Roam, beyond its overall solid reliability, the Roam is a standard mid-tier bike computer. It features a slew of handy navigation features, including turn-by-turn directions, navigate to start, back on track, mountain bike trail integration, saved locations, retrace route, and take me to.

After using the Edge 1050 for almost six months, the best word to describe Garmin’s range-topping computer is “substantial”. This computer is big in size, features, and price. But all of this bigness provides an experience unlike anything found on other cycling computers—and if not for the 1050’s price, it would be vying for the Best Overall Computer title.

Sources indicate that there is no getting around the Edge 1050’s size, and at 2.4” x 4.7” x 0.6”, it takes up a lot of real estate on your bar. In fact, the 105 is so long that it’s incompatible with many standard mounts. However, the enormous size makes it easy to read data, follow routes, and scroll screens.

Navigation features include turn-by-turn directions, maps showing the popular routes locals use, and recalculation when you stray from your course. And while they might not like the 1050’s dimensions, mountain bikers will love its integration with the Trailforks app. However, this is merely scratching the surface of the Edge 1050’s superpowers; if you want to see the data, the 1050 is probably logging it, and Garmin most likely has a screen for it buried in the long list of data fields.

The Edge 1050 also offers some thoughtful safety features, including the ability to automatically send an emergency message to your specified contacts when it detects a crash, group messaging, and a ‘follow my ride’ feature that shares your real-time position with friends and family.

If you like these features but want a smaller package (and slightly lower price), check out the Garmin Edge 850. You can dig into the details on the 850 in Dan Chabanov’s full-length review.

Like Garmin’s Edge 1050, Wahoo goes similarly huge with its Elemnt Ace. The screen’s 3.8-inch size is impressive, as is its battery life (up to 30 hours). Plus, the Ace features Wahoo’s signature user-friendliness. Matt Phillips summed up his full review of the Elemnt Ace, saying, “If you crave significant and bold, this is your cycling computer.”.

Industry observers note that the Ace’s super-sized screen offers room for large and easy-to-read data fields. The touchscreen function is also excellent, even while wearing gloves. Wahoo’s signature page zoom function—use the up and down buttons to zoom in on fewer fields or out on more fields—quickly makes prioritized fields even larger. This helps if you want to concentrate on one metric or have vision challenges. It also provides a very major map (or a large map plus additional data fields) and spoken turn-by-turn directions.

Recent findings suggest that compared to most cycling computers, the Ace is overkill in almost every way. However, if you want one computer with a significant screen and impressive battery life, then the Ace is your ticket.

Do you wax nostalgic for the days of simple cycling computers—but still want to upload your rides and training data to Strava? Then the Omata is the computer for you. Years ago, our computers only displayed the basic riding metrics like speed, ride time, distance, and elevation. Your rides weren’t interrupted by constant pinging from notifications, messages, navigation, and target training zones.

Silca’s Omata computer is to your rides like a vinyl turntable is to listening to music. Sure, you can stream your favorite band on Spotify, see the songs’ lyrics in real time, and skip tracks you don’t like, but digital audio lacks the tactile experience of a record player. That’s what riding with the Omata is like; it features dials to display your current speed, distance traveled, elevation gain, and riding time—nothing more, nothing less.

It has been revealed that yet, behind the scenes, the Omata also captures critical riding data, like power, heart rate, and GPS route. This means you can still track your rides and get Strava kudos from your friends. However, the Omata comes at a steep price—$800—but it‘s an experience you will not find in any other device.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest differences between GPS cycling computers is the technology ecosystem you’re buying into—much like choosing a smartphone. While you can pair most sensors, regardless of brand, with most computers via Bluetooth or ANT+, these devices work best when used with their corresponding companion apps. Although some budget-friendly computer options require an app to unlock full functionality, premium models from brands like Hammerhead, Wahoo, and Garmin let you perform most tasks without an app.

In a recent development, while bigger isn’t always better, a large, easy-to-read display—like the one on the Wahoo Elemnt Ace—makes navigation and data viewing significantly more convenient. When testing the gargantuan Elemnt Ace, Matt Phillips initially found the screen’s sheer size off-putting, but he eventually grew to appreciate it.

Industry observers note that navigation capabilities vary widely. Even budget models, such as the $120 iGPSport BCS300T, support turn-by-turn directions with downloadable routes. High-end models such as the Hammerhead Karoo and Garmin Edge models take it further, allowing on-the-fly route changes—such as finding a coffee shop—without adjusting settings in the companion app.

Industry observers note that battery life used to be a major concern, but modern bike computers are built to last. Most can handle a full week of riding without recharging. Some, like the Coros Dura and Garmin Edge 840 Solar, even feature solar charging. In fact, the Coros Dura’s battery is so robust that some consumers report they haven’t been able to completely drain it after months of use, making its claimed 120-hour battery life seem entirely plausible.

The computers in this story are optimized for cycling and intended for on-bike use. If you participate in events like triathlons or duathlons—or also need a device for running or hiking activities—consider a smartwatch with cycling functionality. Our guide to Garmin watches can help you select the right one for your rides and runs.

With expert instruction from pro rider Chaz Turmon, this program features motivating follow-along video sessions and flexible workouts you can do almost anywhere to help you ride faster, train smarter, and watch your numbers climb.

This holistic program covers all the tips and tricks needed to improve your riding technique, master cadence, stack speed and endurance workouts, build strength off the bike, and fine‑tune gear in order to achieve the speed gains you dream about.

Sources indicate that watch as host Alison Tetrick takes you through everything you need to know to ride your first (or fastest) century. Along with other cycling experts, she explains how to find the best gear, build endurance, fuel your body during the ride, and much more.

Cycling is the best way to stay fit as you age. With the help of host Peter Abraham and other experts, you’ll learn everything you need to get started and stay riding into your golden years, including choosing a bike, finding a plan, and optimizing recovery.

Whether you’re constantly feeling aches or you want to maximize your performance gains, you need the right bike fit. With this guide, host Jenna Foley and certified bike fitter Jonathan Blyer walk you through the process and offer up DIY tips.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Latest England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

What Nike Shoe Matches Your Running Style?

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that runners are a varied breed.
  • In a recent development, luckily, there’s a Nike shoe to support your training goals, whether you run for fun or race competitively.
  • You can depend on your daily run—it’s what gives you energy and lifts your mood, no matter what else the day may bring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that runners are a varied breed. Some crave the routine of a daily run and the endorphin boost it brings. Others may be training for an endurance event like a marathon or half marathon, with specific distance goals. You may be chasing a upcoming PR, looking to hit the trails, or mixing running with other activities like lifting weights. So many different ways to run, so many shoes to choose from.

In a recent development, luckily, there’s a Nike shoe to support your training goals, whether you run for fun or race competitively. Not sure which style fits your needs best? We’ve got you covered with the shopping guide below.

You can depend on your daily run—it’s what gives you energy and lifts your mood, no matter what else the day may bring. The Nike Pegasus line has offered that same dependability for more than four decades, and the technology just keeps getting better.

It has been revealed that the reason why the Pegasus Plus 2 works for daily, all-purpose running is its technology: Superlight ZoomX foam in the heel pairs with an exposed Air Zoom unit in the forefoot to deliver comfort and energy return that powers up every mile. Up top, a sleek mesh material offers both support and flexibility without letting your foot overheat, while a revamped forefoot shape gives your toes a little more wiggle room. And the classic Waffle outsole design has an updated diagonal pattern with flex grooves for better traction and ground feel, so you’re more in tune with your terrain. Plus, those textured laces are less likely to come untied—so you’ve got one less thing to worry about when you’re heading out the door.

Sources indicate that the Pegasus Plus 2 is also a good option to slip on for easy and slower recovery runs. Responsive and comfy without being super stacked, this shoe is the ultimate workhorse in your running closet.

In a recent development, for long runs and marathon training, you want max cushioning, like what’s found in Nike’s Vomero 18. Lightweight ZoomX foam stacked on top of responsive ReactX foam in the shoe’s midsole results in a plushy landing that has you feeling like you’re landing on a cloud with every step. Considering that the Vomero 18 is 13 percent more responsive than previous React technology (per the organization’s own measurement), your legs feel less fatigued even as the miles add up.

Sources indicate that an increased rocker design and pods placed strategically around the outsole allow for better push-off and smoother heel-to-toe transitions. The breathable engineered mesh material up top and plush padding in the tongue and lining help your feet stay cool and comfortable. This super cushy shoe that runs effortlessly is one of the reasons why RW shoe testers gush about it.

For those who like to customize their kicks, the shoe is part of the “Nike by You” line, allowing you to pick features like color and accents and even add your own text in the heel, tongue, and forefoot.

Recent findings suggest that you’re not just a runner. You also rule the weight room, enjoy a good cardio class, and have been known to dabble in metabolic conditioning workouts. If you’re looking for an all-purpose training shoe, Nike’s versatile Free Metcon 7 fits whatever your workout ask. This sleekly designed cross-training shoe lets you have it all, from supporting multi-direction movements on the gym floor to dynamic cushioning when you want to hit the treadmill.

In a recent development, the shoe finds its multiuse purpose with a flexible design that features softer foam in the midsole and firmer foam in the heel for added stability. Plus, the full-length rubber outsole helps with traction on a variety of surfaces, including turf, concrete, and gym floors. You’ll also appreciate the webbed lacing and midfoot containment system designed to keep your foot firmly in place as you move around.

According to recent reports, for those who want a mixed-terrain shoe that can hit the road and trail and also handle inclement weather like rain and snow, the Vomero 18 Gore-Tex is a great choice. These waterproof shoes are designed to take on puddles, pebbles, rocks, and roots without missing a beat.

The shoe has all the same stacked ZoomX and ReactX performance cushioning as the Vomero 18, plus a Gore-Tex waterproof liner to help your feet stay dry without getting too sweaty. The Storm-Tread outsole is specifically engineered for wet and slippery conditions, with an enhanced rubber compound for stronger grip and a thoughtful outsole pattern that keeps you grounded even on icy surfaces. Plus, the soft, protective mesh upper will keep your feet warm.

If you are looking for a shoe to race in, the long-awaited Alphafly 4 is an update to Nike’s popular carbon-plated shoe. It’s even lighter than its predecessor, the Alphafly 3, (approximately 6.6 ounces compared to 7.1 ounces respectively) and offers more energy return to help you chase your next PR.

Sources indicate that that’s accomplished through its upgraded RF Air Zoom cushioning unit underfoot that uses vibration and frequency to create a smooth, comfortable ride, while the carbon fiber Flyplate gives you extra energy return to power through every mile. A slightly wider platform design compared to the Alphafly 3 also provides more stability so you can feel confident even on quick turns. And the wispy Atomknit 2.0 upper offers enough support to keep your foot firmly in place with as little added weight as possible.

Your shakeout run after a marathon or ultra should be about comfort at an easy pace. Think plenty of cushioning, a smooth, bouncy ride, and an unfussy upper. The Nike Vomero Premium ticks all those boxes, making it a good choice to slip on for post-marathon recovery runs.

Sources indicate that tired legs will appreciate a midsole that’s made up of ZoomX foam surrounding two energy-boosting Air Zoom units—one in the forefoot and one at the heel. The result is a light, comfortable ride with energy return that makes each step feel effortless and propels you easily along your route. You’ll want to wear this shoe for your daily runs for weeks after your 26.2-mile-and-beyond races.

In a recent development, who doesn’t want to slip into something comfortable after a long run, or just a long day? The Nike ReactX Rejuven8 is just the thing, with a design that’s created to elicit all the aahs you can imagine. Thanks to React X technology in the upper and midsole, your feet will be surrounded in soft, responsive comfort. There’s extra room in the forefoot to allow your toes to rest and ventilation holes to allow your feet to breathe. Walking is easy and fluid because the sticky rubber outsole adds grip to the ground below you; therefore, no additional balancing act to get from one place to another. The result: A recovery shoe you’ll never want to take off.

We all love getting gifts, but shopping for shoes can be tricky when you’re not the one who will be wearing them. A little advanced knowledge can make a massive difference in ensuring your present is truly appreciated. Here are some buying tips:.

According to recent reports, check what they already run in. If you can, look at the label inside a pair of running shoes they like, or ask someone who knows. Note the model, size, and width—running-shoe sizing may differ from their dress-shoe size—as well as any preferences, such as cushioning or toe-box room.

It has been revealed that check the return policy. See if the store has any specific limits on returns and exchanges, and if you can get a gift receipt so your giftee has the option to exchange the shoe for a different size.

Keep fit in mind. Remember that footwear largely depends on individual fit, with some shoes running bigger or smaller than the given size. When possible, avoid final sales (where the shoe is not eligible for returns) just in case there’s a fit concern.

The Nike running shoes best suited for long runs and marathon training are the Nike Vomero 18. You want to make sure your shoe offers both stability and support to reduce injury risk and protect your joints. Many distance runners today prefer shoes with maximalist midsoles, which feature a large stack of foam to cushion against impact, as well as energy return rocker designs for faster push-off and landings. These are all things the Nike Vomero 18 delivers on.

When it comes to race-day itself, especially for half-marathons and full-marathons, many runners seeking a time goal prefer performance shoes like Nike’s Alphafly 4, which have a thin carbon plate for strong energy return and maximum speed.

When looking for a recovery-run shoe, you want one that feels comfortable and provides plenty of support and a smooth, stable ride without being overly technical. The Nike Vomero Premium is the best Nike running shoe for easy recovery runs because it’s a shoe that delivers full-length cushioning and a roomy fit so your feet stay happy.

It has been revealed that to choose the right size and width for Nike running shoes, go to a store that specializes in running shoes and try a few pairs on. Most running stores will let you jog around the floor (and some even let you jog around the block) so you have a sense of what works best. Running shoes should feel roomy but not so much that your feet move around a lot. You should be able to fit about a thumbnail’s width between your longest toe and the front of the shoe. There also shouldn’t be any pressure on your pinky toe, and only a little bit of pressure on your significant toe.

If you’re experiencing side pinching, bulging or spilling over, or flat arches, a wide shoe may be for you. These Nike models are available in wide widths: Downshifter 14, Pegasus 42, Revolution 8, Structure 26, Vomero Plus and Vomero 18.

Recent findings suggest that A good pair of mountain bike shorts should stay out of your way through long climbs, rough descents, and everything in between. The right fit leaves room to pedal and wear knee pads without bunching or snagging, while a secure waistband and well-placed pockets keep the shorts comfortable on the trail. We’ve tested options for different budgets and riding styles, from lightweight shells to shorts with a padded liner. These are the pairs we’d choose for our next ride.

According to recent reports, the Pearl Izumi Summit Shorts scored well across the board, with a comfortable fit, effective water repellency, and well-placed pockets. At 191 grams, they’re relatively light and breathe well (though the Velocio Ultralight MTB Shorts below are yet lighter and more breathable). The Summits still move enough air for all-day trail rides without noticeable moisture buildup.

Industry observers note that their four-way-stretch ripstop nylon has held up through multiple seasons of testing and riding, resisting tears without feeling rough or abrasive. For nylon, it’s surprisingly soft.

Sources indicate that A lined mountain bike short at this price is rare. The Ally has a forgiving fit and plenty of waist adjustment (Velcro sizing tabs and belt loops), which makes it easier to wear than many shorts. On the bike they feel relaxed and comfortable (but not floppy), and move with you well. The included liner means you don’t need to buy a chamois separately. Plenty of pockets let you stash a phone and ride essentials, though all those zippers can feel like a lot—and like potential failure points over time. The unisex sizing means there’s no separate women’s version.

Industry observers note that with a 13-inch inseam in the men’s version, the Landfarer covers the tops of most knee pads without feeling heavy. The stretch fabric is lightweight, and the broad range of men’s and women’s sizes makes it easier to find a good fit. Patagonia also uses recycled nylon in the fabric and makes the shorts in a Fair Trade Certified™ factory, so the vibes are good. The range of waist sizes can help you find a tailored fit, but the elastic waistband has no adjusters. The low-friction fabric and forgiving waist can let the shorts slip more easily, so make sure you get the right size.

Recent findings suggest that the Ultralight lives up to its name. It’s extremely light and quick-drying, with a cut and fit dialed for long days with lots of pedaling. Despite the light material, these have proven surprisingly durable, shrugging off slides and brushes with rocks and trailside vegetation. I tested the latest version, which features a new elastic waist that greatly improved the fit and made it more forgiving of weight fluctuations. One caveat: that waistband change appears to be rolling through production, so not all pairs and colors have the new waist yet. These are also expensive.

The Flexair keeps things low-key and streamlined. Its low-profile cut and ratchet closure make for a clean look and a secure fit on the bike. The leg opening sits close to the thigh, so these work best with very low-profile knee pads; bulkier pads may feel crowded. Stretch fabric and laser-cut perforations help keep the shorts light and ventilated, but there’s no liner. The waists run small, so try them on if you can and be prepared to size up.

According to recent reports, there are plenty of great bike shorts out there—but most of them play it safe with earth tones and muted colors. Wild Rye bucks that trend. This women-led brand out of Sun Valley, ID makes technical “apparel that inspires more women to get outside”—and look good doing it. The standout designs and bold colors are just as impressive as the performance of the gear itself. If you want high-quality apparel with flair and personality, this is your brand.

The Riley 10” Bike Short checks all the right boxes. A high-rise waist prevents sagging in the back while riding, and a stretch panel across the rear waistband adds comfort and flexibility. Along with a side zip pocket that fits a phone, the shorts also have two front pockets for smaller essentials. The 10-inch inseam will suit most riders, though it may not pair perfectly with all knee pads.

Pro tip: Check the sale page for deals on last year’s designs.

A firm that builds only women’s athletic apparel typically nails it in every category, and these super-comfortable, breezy shell shorts from Shredly are no exception. With a versatile 11” inseam and a wide, high, soft waistband, these pair really well with a slightly longer chamois liner or waist shorts, and sit high on the waist to reduce gapping during rides.

The shorts material has 9 percent spandex for structure and four-way stretch that lends maximum range of motion. These are built for a woman’s hips and waist, and have an articulated taper that doesn’t impede pedaling.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

The 8 Best Treadmills of 2026

📅 21 May 2018 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Before you get on the treadmill hate train, hear me out.
  • There are a ton of treadmills on the market right now, and they’re better than they’ve ever been.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Before you get on the treadmill hate train, hear me out. They can save your training, and I swear, they can be a ton of fun—really. Between the engaging, interactive streaming treadmill classes, and the ability to strip down to your skivvies and have no one see you sweat, it’s the perfect accompaniment to your marathon training, interval workouts, and even steady, zone 2 workouts. All from the comfort of your own home. And did you know that with many insurance aims, you can pay for your treadmill with FSA dollars? That’s a solid fiscal choice, right there.

There are a ton of treadmills on the market right now, and they’re better than they’ve ever been. They have more features, use less electricity, and are more versatile than ever before. Some are virtually personal trainers in and of themselves.

We’re in the process of testing a few newly introduced models, and we’ve just added the Urevo CyberMega, which is the first treadmill designed specifically for marathon training. It’s pretty freaking sick, I cannot lie.

According to recent reports, looking for a more heavy-duty treadmill that can handle higher speeds, longer miles, and more complex training looks? See our guide for the best advanced treadmills, which cost more but offer more training features and sturdier builds.

According to recent reports, there’s really something special about this machine. The NordicTrack Commercial 1750 treadmill hits that “Goldilocks-level” sweet spot with its cushioning—it’s responsive enough to save your joints without making your run feel like a slog or an unstable adventure. And with a 60-inch belt, even our tallest testers with their gazelle-like strides had plenty of room to stretch out and feel steady.

Recent findings suggest that our testers absolutely gushed over the treadmill’s sleek, streamlined design, especially the Z-shaped console with its high-perched 16-inch screen. It’s perfectly positioned for runners who like to stay close to the controls. While we wished the cup holders were a bit deeper for our oversized water bottles, the slim arms offered a surprisingly stable grip, even when our hands got a little… enthusiastic.

The 1750’s speed adjustments are pretty standard, going from 6 mph to a zippy 12 mph in 8 seconds. This is totally fine for 400- to 800-meter training, but for intense, quick-pickup speedwork, it’s not quite as snappy as some might like. Our testers did note one minor peeve: the lack of quick keys for 10 and 11 mph.

We practically insist you dive into NordicTrack’s iFit program for an out-of-this-world experience. Our testers found its ability to read and adjust their runs to be nothing short of revolutionary during testing. While the high horsepower motor and Bluetooth speakers do make the machine a bit boisterous, it’s not at all distracting when you’re walking with your headphones on.

Sources indicate that despite its daunting price tag, the 1750 is a total workhorse that will supercharge your runs—and it goes on sale often. The built-in Netflix feature is a godsend, making miles absolutely fly by, and that cushioning is pure magic for your joints. Bottom line: the NordicTrack Commercial 1750 is a fantastic all-around package and a top-notch investment for most runners.

NordicTrack Commercial 1750 Review.

The Horizon T101 treadmill proves you don’t need a huge budget for a fantastic workout. At a sale price of just $600, this compact folding machine impressed us with consistent performance over weeks of testing. It’s a low-to-the-ground, 20- by 55-inch deck, ideal for casual runners 6 feet and under.

Recent findings suggest that the T101 boasts a three-zone running surface, offering extra cushioning where you land, less where you toe off, and a smooth transition in between for a supremely comfortable, low-impact ride. While it skips the fancy screens, its functionality shines. Connect to Strava or Peloton, or dive into workouts and courses via the free atZone app. Plus, there’s a perfect spot for your iPad to stream your favorite highlights!

Recent findings suggest that the six built-in programs are straightforward, displaying calories burned, heart rate, distance, speed, and incline (up to 10 percent). While it can hit a 6-minute mile, be mindful: the speed and incline dials are sensitive—one haptic notch, not a full spin, increases your pace.

Recent findings suggest that but you know what’s a real showstopper? The T101’s incredibly easy, one-step hydraulic fold. Just lift the back, and it zips up. To release, toe the center bar, and it gently lowers itself.

Industry observers note that for its price, the T101’s features are unbeatable. It’s not for marathoners or speed demons, but for everyone else, it’s a solid win.

Horizon’s 7.0 folding treadmill is a robust upgrade, boasting a spacious 60-inch deck perfect for long strides, though its 20-inch width might feel snug if your mind wanders. Cushioning is excellent for long runs, but expect some bounce when the incline exceeds 5 percent—so perhaps skip the speedy hill work.

It has been revealed that this machine is on the bulkier side, resembling a gym-quality unit, but its integrated features ensure easy setup. We loved the eye-level tablet holder, making streaming a breeze. Below, you’ll find a digital/manual console, fan, Bluetooth speakers, and two generously wide (if shallow) cup holders with room for your essentials.

Programming-wise, the 7.0 shines with its ability to link to Peloton, Apple Watch, and Samsung Galaxy watches, displaying calories and distance directly. Peloton classes synced smoothly, making transitions seamless.

Sources indicate that A standout feature: knobs on the grips allow for effortless pace adjustments without breaking your stride. While there’s a subtle lag when decreasing speed, it’s barely noticeable at top speeds.

At around $1,000 on sale, this treadmill offers impressive value. Its blend of convenience and comfort makes it a winner. Pro tip: opt for white-glove delivery—this beast is heavy, and assembly is a pain!

Full Horizon 7.0 AT Treadmill Review.

It has been revealed that marathon training demands months of relentless mileage, a crap ton of structured workouts, and more consistency than most of us think we’re capable of. The Urevo CyberMega is a treadmill that claims to be built specifically for the rigors of that beast of blocks. In a market crowded with all-purpose machines designed to serve everyone from casual walkers to occasional joggers to high-mileage baddies, the CyberMega is thinking of the needs of marathon runners first.

In a recent development, that marathon-focused idea makes the entire experience. Rather than treating running as just one feature among many, the CyberMega is designed around the realities of high-volume training. According to the brand, every aspect of the machine is intended to support athletes preparing for long-distance races, making it a notably different proposition from traditional fitness-focused treadmills.

There are marathon courses built into the app that control your ‘mill, there’s AI coaching to get you to your PR, and a fun competitive leaderboard where you are up against other customers. This treadmill is made to keep your training going when you can’t get outside and also? To keep it exciting. It is honestly fairly impressive and a ton of fun to run on.

I was also impressed by how smooth the run is and how compact the machine is. It folds easily, stores without much hassle, and feels dang streamlined for a treadmill made to support hardcore training. That’s also the biggest drawback. If you’re over 6 feet tall, this is not the ‘mill for you with a 52-inch-long deck. But in spite of the short deck, it landed on this list is because it’s a wide-open area that doesn’t feel impeded by the bars.

Recent findings suggest that the rotary knob is another nifty feature. It’s simple, responsive, and super convenient during workouts, and has speed and incline adjustments feeling smoother and more intuitive than traditional button-based controls or rocker dials. Overall, if you’re gonna be a world major chaser, you might want to think about chasing them on this ‘mill.

Got a few runners in the family, or you’re a high-mileage runner? The NordicTrack 2450 is a seriously solid folding treadmill that’s got your back. It’s built tough, has great cushioning, and a huge 22-by-60-inch running surface, so you can just run without worrying about comfort and stability.

The Z-shaped handlebar and crossbar design are super minimalist, keeping the console right there when you need it, and giving you plenty of room to stretch out at the front of the belt.

You’ve got your standard speed and incline adjustments, and this baby can zoom from 6 to 14 mph in under 10 seconds—perfect for those quick interval bursts. It has those quick keys like the 1750, but sometimes it can be a little tricky to nail down specific speeds.

Industry observers note that where the NordicTrack really shines is its iFit programming. We’re talking thousands of workouts, even marathon courses! Yeah, it’s an extra cost, but seriously, it’s a huge motivator. And that big display? It’s awesome. You can pause your run to squeeze in some strength training or even stream your favorite demonstrates.

Recent findings suggest that fair warning, though: putting this thing together is a beast, so you might want to call in a pro. And while it’s not super loud, it might be a bit disruptive if you’re trying to sneak in an early morning workout while everyone else is still snoozing.

The ProForm Carbon TLX is a robust and dependable treadmill, designed for those who appreciate solid performance over excessive features. Its simplicity allows for focused workouts, minimizing distractions so you can stay in tune with your run. While it offers connectivity for phones, tablets, and fitness apps like iFit, at its core, the Carbon TLX is a workhorse—a no-fuss machine ready for you to hop on, get your miles in, and hop off.

The treadmill features a responsive and cushioned surface that offers a pleasant bounce at higher speeds. Our testers found that despite the softer feel, the generous 60- by 20-inch deck allowed for a natural stride. However, I did occasionally feel myself drawing closer to the front console, so if you prefer more forward space, a different model might be better suited.

Sources indicate that for speed enthusiasts, the Carbon TLX is a dream. It rapidly reaches its top speed of 12 mph, and manual buttons provide smooth transitions between speeds. The incline goes up to 12 percent, providing a challenging workout that feels surprisingly good, even uphill. A standout feature is the powerful fan, strategically placed to provide excellent airflow—a detail any woman who’s done the “lift the boobs to get air” maneuver will appreciate.

If you’re a first-time treadmill buyer or looking to stay within budget, the Carbon TLX offers exceptional value for its price.

The Bowflex T9 treadmill brings a punch of fun and functionality to home workouts, making it a standout pick for casual runners and fitness fans alike. The red center line on the belt isn’t just for show—it helps wandering runners stay in their lane, so every jog feels more confident (and a little less wobbly). The running surface is firm and comfortable, with just enough pep to keep things lively, while the compact, foldable design slides neatly out of the way after your workout adventure.

The controls and incline? Well, they’re not winning any races. Adjustments take their time, so interval chasers might grumble about holding down those buttons like they’re cranking up a jack-in-the-box. But the T9 redeems itself with robust app compatibility—it syncs up with Peloton, Zwift, and even Apple Watch for gadget lovers, and has an oversized tablet holder for serious streaming or stats-watching mid-run.

Weighing in with a 350-pound weight capacity, a quiet motor, and speed toggles at your fingertips, this treadmill turns everyday training into smooth sailing. It may not be a speed demon, but the T9’s thoughtful features combine comfort and tech for an overall enjoyable ride.

The Echelon Stride 6 is the treadmill I’ve kept at home after running over 1,200 miles on dozens of machines testing them for this article. It’s a solid, foldable treadmill that fits well in small spaces without feeling cramped. The larger-than-expected deck is 20.5 by 60 inches, giving plenty of room for a natural stride, even at my height of 6 feet. The deck provides firm cushioning that’s comfortable but not overly soft, which I definitely prefer for a closer to road-like feel.

Industry observers note that the fold-flat design is a major bonus. The mill is stupid easy to tuck away under a bed or stand upright in a closet or—how I do it—up against a wall behind a curtain. That remarked, it’s heavy when folded upright, so moving it alone can be a pain. The treadmill has a powerful built-in fan and heart rate sensors, nice extras for longer sessions.

Overall, the Stride 6 isn’t flashy or cushioned like some high-end models, but it delivers a dependable run and great space-saving convenience. For a runner who values a firm deck, quiet motor, and compact footprint, it’s a practical choice that keeps me coming back.

Not everyone needs a treadmill for running, and we get that. Sometimes, what you need is access to movement and the ability to stay active all day long. Enter the Go Plus under-desk walking pad. It is the bridge between daily life and running.

I love using this walking pad when I am working. It’s calm and quiet, but allows me to keep my body and brain active when I'd otherwise be sedentary. It has a deck that is a wonderful size to fit under your standing desk, though I do think it could be just a teeny bit wider. It’s only about 50 pounds, and has wheels so you can maneuver it around your space easily. It’s remote-controlled for easy use, and best of all? You can store this gal vertically in your closet. (Just don’t forget about it in there!).

Sources indicate that each and every treadmill on this list has been thoroughly evaluated by our team of editors at Runner’s World. I have personally tested each and every ‘mill on this list. Additionally, we solicited input from other staff at our office, like News Editor Theo Kahler, who has a PR of 14:20 in the 5K.

According to recent reports, the team and I evaluated each treadmill, running for miles in every conceivable combination of uses. We evaluated how they feel, how well they change speeds and inclines, and even how they sound when they’re running. I then gauged that performance against their prices, customer service, and setup and delivery.On that note: I know that not everyone who runs is going to be able to move around a piece of equipment that weighs hundreds of pounds. As someone with a partially paralyzed left hand, I cannot handle the setup and assembly of a treadmill, so good customer service is a highly important factor. I want to make sure that you’re not just getting a good ’mill, but a good overall experience.

Apart from general treadmill safety, there are a few questions you need to ask yourself before you buy the treadmill. These include how you want to use it, how long your stride is, if you want entertainment or training built in, and what you need as far as weight limits are concerned.

Recent findings suggest that having a comfortable treadmill means having one with a deck large enough to suit your stride. You don’t want to feel like you’re chasing to stay near the bar and not slip off the back, and you should ensure it’s wide enough that you can shake into your run without concern that you’ll step off the belt.

Industry observers note that having a running surface at least 20 inches wide is the bare minimum, and only for runners and walkers who have a consistent gait and few distractions when they run. It’s great for space to have a slimmer belt, but like running on a narrow trail, it requires concentration.

Recent findings suggest that the length of the deck is a trickier problem. What you need is largely dependent on the length of your stride, where you like to land in relation to your center of gravity, and your height/limb length. Having a deck that is too short puts you at risk for falling. Alternatively, it might have you trying to run up against the bar, which can affect your cadence and speed work, as you are essentially trying to outrun the machine instead of following its speed.

It has been revealed that if you’re planning on using the treadmill for running, you’re going to want at least 55 inches of deck length. If you’re just using it for walking, 45 to 50 inches should suffice.

Sources indicate that if you’ve ever uttered the word “fartlek” out loud, you, my friend, need a treadmill that has easily adjustable speeds, and many of them at that. Do you need it to go all the way up to 12 miles per hour (generally the fastest speed on any treadmill) to hit that 5-minute mile? Probably not, but you at least want it to hit your top speed, and you want it to do it smoothly and easily.

Running is a sport of efficiency, and having to stop just to punch buttons that are not immediately responsive or are difficult to find will take away from your training.

It has been revealed that incline training is great for a lot of reasons, not least of which is preparing to run a hilly course. The majority of commercial treadmills offer some level of incline capability. Higher end models can reach a maximum of a 15 degree incline, designed to test the limits of your quads and glutes. Some models also give you the ability to do the opposite—offering decline modes—but those are pretty rare.

It has been revealed that treadmills offer more programming and entertainment than ever. Treadmills are no longer just a belt, motor, and bar. They are now Wi-Fi-compatible machines with programming capable of creating entire running aims and helping you execute them.

On-board systems like NordicTrack’s iFit are designed to help runners (and walkers) on their journey by providing them with tools like heart-rate monitor based workouts, whole-body fitness programs for runners, and responsive tech that monitors intensity, adjusting for your needs as you go.

And perhaps more importantly for many of us, a lot of treadmills can connect to streaming services like Netflix, Spotify, Hulu, and more. Nothing will get you running quite so fast as watching Annabelle while you’re hitting your miles (though it may artificially elevate your heart rate, causing the machine to tell you to slow down).

Motors are a critical element to the design and function of the treadmill. There are typically two motors on each treadmill—one for running the belt and one to power the incline. The motor running the belt is the one taking the heaviest damage and using the greatest amount of energy, so it needs to be robust.

Speed and motors are closely related—in order to give the user an option to hit higher speeds, the treadmill needs a strong motor to keep up. Most motors are between 1.5 and 4 horsepower. We should note that the majority of treadmills with higher weight limits (north of 300 pounds) tend to have higher horsepower.

In a recent development, we have found in our testing that higher-power motors can also take a lot more abuse, staying right and ready for more miles. Unfortunately, this does typically mean that the treadmill itself may be more expensive, but for larger-bodied individuals, distance runners, or speed runners, it’s worth the cost of admission.

What are the potential benefits for walking or running on a treadmill versus outdoors?

Recent findings suggest that it’s predictable. Greer says that it “allows the runner to precisely set and control all parameters, including speed, incline, and duration. This is especially beneficial for walkers or runners who are systematically progressing back into activity, either after injury, time away, latest to running, or runners completing a specific workout.”.

In a recent development, it also helps you stay consistent, which is critical when training. “Given the benefits of accessibility and predictability, a treadmill can help to promote a more consistent exercise routine.”.

What are some of the potential risks of treadmill training/use?

There are risks for specific treadmill injuries. “Recent literature indicates some differences in biomechanics between running on a treadmill vs overground. Differences in biomechanics result in tissues being loaded differently, specifically increased loading of the Achilles tendon with treadmill running.”.

Industry observers note that when you run outdoors, your body encounters different obstacles that help strengthen it. “Walking/running on the treadmill does not allow the diversification of movements and muscle activity required in comparison to outdoor walking/running. For example, up/down hills, turning, stepping onto curb or over puddle.”.

You might exert yourself more. There is evidence to suggest that “runners report a higher rate of perceived exertion (RPE) when running on a treadmill vs overground.”.

Industry observers note that you need to know yourself and your limits to be safe. “Treadmills allow the walker/runner to easily increase the belt speed, however, make sure the speed does not exceed that which you are able to run safe and that you can continue to run with your normal running mechanics.”.

Tips for safe treadmill training?

Sources indicate that treadmills are a massive piece of exercise equipment, and they can be dangerous if not installed properly and monitored when in use. That is why we spoke with Ed Pryts, chief sales officer at Gym Source, a 30-year treadmill industry veteran, to learn the most important safety factors before you purchase a fresh treadmill for your home.

In a recent development, cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and right now studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

Industry observers note that jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

The Best Bike Helmets of 2026: 14 Editor-Tested Picks Starting at Only $30
