💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, bicycle helmets have saved my life more times than I can count.
  • In a recent development, while some lids from decades past were bulky and sometimes looked silly, modern road, mountain, and commuter helmets combine safety, performance, and style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

According to recent reports, bicycle helmets have saved my life more times than I can count. I’ve ridden and raced bikes for most of my life, so unfortunately I’ve hit the deck many times on trails and on roads. That’s why I wear a helmet anytime I kit up, clip in, and head out for a ride.

In a recent development, while some lids from decades past were bulky and sometimes looked silly, modern road, mountain, and commuter helmets combine safety, performance, and style. While a helmet’s primary role is to protect your head and brain in a crash, the best bike helmets also look great, and some even improve your speed.

Helmet technology has improved considerably in the last decade. Plus, safety features once limited to high-end helmets have trickled down to affordable models. Rider safety has also improved: independent testing by Virginia Tech has prompted more manufacturers to incorporate anti-rotational features across all helmet styles, categories, and price levels. Additionally, high-tech materials, improved ventilation, better straps, and more aerodynamic shapes make today’s lids lighter, cooler, and faster than those from only a few years ago.

Picking the perfect helmet can be challenging. Brands offer scores of models in every possible riding category. Whether you ride on asphalt, gravel roads, or dirt trails, you can find a helmet that matches your style, fit, and budget needs.

Expert Advice: Buy the helmet that feels the most comfortable on your head. You are more likely to use a helmet that fits and feels great, and that’s the first step in keeping your noggin safe if you crash.

Elite road and gravel helmets offer low weight, excellent ventilation, and great looks. However, those benefits usually come at a high cost. Giro’s Agilis Mips helmet is a great option if you want a pro-level look and performance without the associated price.

Weighing 299 grams (size medium), my Agilis is only 15 grams heavier than Giro’s premium Aries Spherical model—and the Agilis costs $230 less. The Agilis is very well-ventilated, comparable to the priciest lids on all but the hottest of rides.

It has been revealed that giro offers eight color options for the Agilis, so you’re sure to find one that matches your riding kits, bike, and personal style. This helmet features Mips technology to protect your brain from rotational forces in a crash, and Giro’s Hardbody co-molded shell to better protect it from small bumps and dings when not on your head. Plus, the Agilis is equipped with Roc-Loc dial system to ensure a proper fit.

Recent findings suggest that with a five-star rating and 8.14 STAR score, the P2R A20 Mips places third in Virginia Tech’s road helmet rankings (and eleventh overall). That ranking is great for any road or gravel helmet—but for a helmet that costs only $60, it’s downright amazing.

In a recent development, P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting many corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road. The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it remarked the A20 fits a little snug near their temples.

TOP 5 RANKED VA TECH ROAD HELMETS.

Although it costs less than $80, I reach for the Lazer Tonic KinetiCore as often as helmets triple its price. The Tonic looks good and fits great, and at only 247 grams, it’s lighter than many more expensive lids I own. Plus, it features 18 vents for good airflow on hot days. Another thing I like about the Tonic KinetiCore is the options: Lazer offers it in nine colors and four sizes. This means you’re almost guaranteed to find one that fits your head and personal style.

Overall, the Tonic KinetiCore looks, feels, and rides like much pricier helmets. It combines low weight, ventilation, and protection into an affordable package. The Tonic uses Lazer’s proprietary KinetiCore system; it reduces weight and integrates rotational impact protection. This is a solid lid for your daily road and gravel rides or even commutes.

Recent findings suggest that for the Aries Spherical, Giro improved ventilation and aerodynamics over its previous range-topping Aether model. It is an excellent, pro-level road lid for road riders seeking superior performance and fit. It’s lightweight, super-adjustable, and is offered in tons of colors—including Visma-Lease a Bike and Canyon-SRAM special editions.

In a recent development, the Aries also has excellent safety features—I know how well the Aries Spherical works because I personally crash-tested it late last year. Giro incorporates its Spherical nested-shell (ball-in-socket) design for rotational-force protection in a crash and improved energy dissipation. The Aries also uses Giro’s Aura reinforcement bridges to keep the foam in place during impact. These features earned the Aries an excellent five-star rating from Virginia Tech. It ranks in the top fifteen overall and fifth in road helmets.

It has been revealed that the Smith Network Mips employs many features from the manufacturer’s pricier models, along with some truly novel ones. It retains the honeycomb-like Koroyd panels that absorb energy upon impact. The Network also features an optional fabric visor for the convenience of a cycling cap without the added bulk.

Since Smith (a sunglass company) makes this helmet, it has great eyewear integration. Color options are another upside to the Network; there is one to match virtually any rider’s style.

P2R’s A70 Pro is probably the best deal for a performance road helmet. At only $100, the A70 punches well above its price. It packs the fit, finish, and adjustability we expect from much pricier lids. Plus, this P2R helmet features a Mips liner and earned a four-star rating from Virginia Tech’s helmet lab.

Recent findings suggest that for the price, it’s an excellent helmet, but it has a few downsides. While it wasn’t noticeable while riding, the A70 Pro is a bit heavier than competitors’ pricier aero helmets. Fit-wise, the A70 fit our test riders’ medium-sized heads, but medium is the smallest size available. Lastly, we lost two pairs of glasses from the helmet’s sunglass port, so maybe don’t use that feature.

It has been revealed that aero helmets are a good way to save watts and boost your speed. That’s why you see so many pro racers choosing these sleek lids, even on the warmest days of Grand Tour events. Giro’s new Eclipse Pro is one of the best choices available, and one of the year’s hottest pieces of cycling equipment.

According to recent reports, weighing 280 grams (claimed), the Eclipse Pro is light for an aero helmet, and competes with some brands’ lightweight models. And thanks to improved aerodynamics, Giro claims the Pro is 17% faster than its predecessor, the Eclipse Spherical. Giro also packs the Eclipse Pro with safety features, including its Spherical (anti-rotational), Aura II (reinforcement), and Progressive Layering (dual-density EPS foam) technologies.

Riding POC’s Cytal Mips in 100-degree heat on Stage 5 of the 2026 Tour de France, I learned first-hand how well this helmet ventilates your head. Senior Photographer Trevor Raab backed up my findings in his test riding. He mentioned, “On fast-paced hot rides, it offered a noticeable increase in cooling as well as remaining comfortable while slowly slogging up climbs.”.

In a recent development, like other POC helmets, the Cytal combines Scandinavian style and excellent safety into one package. Although the Cytal’s fit runs large, it’s easy to dial in with its adjustable retention system and different padding options. Raab has an approximately 58cm head and falls between sizes (medium and large). Similarly, I consistently wear a size medium from other brands and found the medium was a little large on my head. If you can size down, it may offer a more streamlined and aero fit.

It has been revealed that expert Advice: Most riders know they should replace a helmet after they crash. But did you know that your helmet can expire? Helmets don’t have an actual best-by date, but the general rule of thumb is to replace your lid every three to five years. So, if you’re wondering, “When did I get this helmet?”, it might be time to replace it.

TLD’s full-face helmets have been the go-to choice of top downhill, freeride, and enduro riders for decades. Since launching the A1 trail helmet more than ten years ago, Troy Lee Designs has led the mountain bike market in comfort, fit, and style. The A3 Mips, the brand’s top-tier trail helmet, takes what makes TLD lids legendary to a latest level.

Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips has ridden the A3 for countless hours on the trails of Durango, Colorado, and gives it a ringing endorsement. He says, “The TLD A3, since its launch a couple of years ago, has risen to the top of my favorite MTB helmets list. The style and color options are a highlight, of course—it’s a TLD. But what makes this helmet a standout is its secure fit and comfort. It locks onto my head and doesn’t wiggle or bounce, yet produces no pressure points. I also appreciate the adjustable visor when the sun is low (or high), reasonably solid eyewear docking, and the super-effective sweat-diverting brow strip, which keeps glasses and goggles dry.”.

Smith recently launched the Pilot, and for only $95, it’s a great overall package. The Pilot features Mips protection, a fit dial, and lightweight straps. The helmet also has great compatibility with glasses and goggles (which only seems right considering eyewear brand Smith makes it). Senior Photographer Trevor Raab tested the Pilot and provided some ride notes.

“Helmets can get expensive, and there are lots of premium features driving the price up on MTB lids. The Pilot gives you everything you need and nothing you don’t without breaking the bank,” Raab said. He additionally notes that “the straps with adjusters that wouldn't seem out of place on helmets costing 2x the price.” The only drawback he has found is the Pilot’s fixed visor: “For those who like to fine-tune their peak, it’s a bit of a drag, but I’m not complaining at this price.”.

The Schwinn Intercept is a $30 helmet and is ranked four stars in Virginia Tech’s STAR testing. That’s a higher ranking than several helmets that VA Tech tested, some of which cost hundreds of dollars more. Though it’s inexpensive, the Interceptor still features a dial-adjustable fit system and a removable visor. It’s a one-size-fits-most model with a claimed weight of about 350 grams—surprisingly light for an affordable helmet.

Recent findings suggest that finding a trail-style mountain bike helmet that looks good, has a 5-star rating from Virginia Tech, and is priced less than $100 is a tall order. However, Endura pulled it together with its Hummveee Mips model.

Sources indicate that british-brand Endura is best-known for its excellent riding apparel, but its mountain bike helmets are also worth a look. The Hummvee features a Mips liner to protect against rotational forces in a crash, a removable visor, and in-mold construction to improve durability. While it’s a one-size-fits-most helmet, Endura offers this lid in three color choices: black, red, and white.

If you’re commuting by e-bike, you’ll want to wear a helmet. However, not all commuter lids are rated for e-bike use. Unit 1’s Aura smart helmet not only passes NTA8776 and EN1078 safety standards, but it also earned a five-star rating from Virginia Tech’s helmet lab and ranks third among all commuter helmets.

The Aura also has several built-in features to increase your visibility to drivers. These include 350-lumen head and taillights, turn signals, crash detection, and a Fidlock buckle. It even pairs with Bosch e-bikes.

Sources indicate that this tech comes at a price—in both dollars and grams. At $260, it’s not the cheapest commuter helmet, but it’s arguably the best equipped. The Aura’s 469-gram weight (measured, size medium) is noticeable while riding, and it can feel a little heavy the first few times you wear it.

Inspired by vintage motorcycle helmets, the Thousand Heritage is trendy and comfortable. Recently updated, the Heritage 2.0 retains its faux-leather strap and now features larger vents on the top and in the back to keep you cool. It also has a rear dial so you can adjust the fit for your head shape and hairstyle, and we had no trouble managing the helmet’s magnetic buckle with just one hand. The Heritage’s logo also hides a unique feature: It pops off to reveal a small channel through which you can run a lock to secure the helmet. This is handy if you don’t want to carry your lid around once you reach your destination.

Our team thoroughly vetted each helmet on this list. Collectively, we log tens of thousands of miles each year wearing these helmets (and dozens more), in all kinds of conditions. Our test team rides on pavement and gravel, trail rides and bike park laps, daily commutes, and quick spins around town.

Recent findings suggest that we evaluated each helmet based on performance, value, fit, comfort, ventilation, aerodynamics, adjustability, and looks. We also consider Virginia Tech safety ratings when available. The result is a selection of helmets that deliver the best experience across every budget and riding style.

Industry observers note that you probably already know where you like to ride. Perhaps you ride on paved roads, or maybe on gravel and dirt. Other cyclists prefer riding mountain bikes in the woods or on the rail trail with the family.

According to recent reports, helmets are generally grouped by cycling discipline—road, gravel, mountain, commuting, or recreational. But don’t feel boxed in by those labels—You can wear a mountain bike lid for gravel rides, commute in a lightweight road helmet, or don a commuter helmet for weekend rides on the bike path. The best helmet is the one that you will wear—something that fits well, feels good, and meets your budget.

However, it’s still helpful to understand what those category designations actually mean in terms of helmet features, ventilation, and protection:.

You can spend as little as $30 for a helmet or more than $400 on a high-end race lid. Generally, pricier helmets are lighter and better ventilated. However, all helmets sold in the U.S. must meet the same CPSC safety standards.

Industry observers note that for a deep dive into Virginia Tech’s independent helmet testing program, read Matt Phillip’s excellent story, “Virginia Tech’s New Helmet Ratings Raise the Bar. Here’s How the Tougher System Could Affect Your Next Choice.”.

Sources indicate that all helmets sold in the U.S. must meet a Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standard. However, the standard was adopted in 1998. For example, it does not give specifics for mitigating rotational forces on the brain. It also does not lay down any standards for a full-face helmet’s chin bar.

In a recent development, voluntary and third-party tests go beyond the CPSC standard. We like Virginia Tech’s STAR tests, which were developed with a more modern understanding of head injuries than the CPSC’s test. VA Tech’s protocols evaluate a helmet’s ability to mitigate linear acceleration and rotational velocity, then assign a ranking of zero to five stars. A helmet receives more stars if Virginia Tech’s testing indicates it does a better job of reducing injury. VA Tech only recommends helmets that receive four or five stars.

Outside of CPSC and VA Tech’s STAR, most reputable helmet makers have their own in-house test protocols. The specifics of those tests and the results are often proprietary and not shared with the public.

It has been revealed that remember, no controlled test can replicate every possible real-world crash, but wearing a helmet is always better than not wearing one. Additionally, manufacturers’ understanding of what makes an effective helmet improves every day, which means helmets are always improving.

Sizes vary by brand, and most companies offer fit guides to help you choose the best size for your head. Measure your head’s circumference to determine the best size. If you fall between sizes, choose the most comfortable helmet.

Industry observers note that the correct size helmet will sit low and straight on your forehead. The retention system should take up some of the slack so the helmet sits securely on your head—you shouldn’t rely on cinching down the chin strap to hold the helmet in place. The right helmet will fit comfortably, and the retention system will easily snug up the fit.

Consider these other factors when choosing and purchasing a newly introduced helmet.

Typically, road helmets are the lightest and best ventilated helmets. In some cases, the vents even also enhance cooling (over wearing no helmet at all) by directing airflow through carefully designed shapes and vents and over your head. This also helps prevent your sunglasses from fogging. Other helmets with increased coverage, such as full-face and mountain bike helmets, often have fewer vents.

Industry observers note that however, don’t get tricked into thinking that “more vents are better.” You can’t judge a helmet’s cooling ability only by its number of vents. The Giro Synthe, for example, has only 19 vents but is widely regarded as well-ventilated, while the Kask Valegro has a whopping 37 vents. The size and design of the vents, plus thoughtful internal channels, are more important than the quantity.

Recent findings suggest that weight needn’t be your biggest concern because when it comes to a helmet, the one you wear will always win out over the one you don’t. It comes down to comfort—you’re more likely to wear a helmet that won’t get in the way or weigh you down.

Lightweight helmets tend to feel more comfortable, especially on long or challenging rides. Both material choices and design aspects contribute to weight savings. High-tech helmets often save grams by incorporating intricate internal bridges and supports that allow airflow and keep the helmet together in a crash. But be prepared to pay a higher price for these innovations. Opting out of “extras” like visors and mounts will also reduce weight.

While we don’t recommend adorning your helmet with too many accessories, extras such as visors, GoPro mounts, and lights certainly have their place and time.

Recent findings suggest that if you find yourself riding in the dark, light mounts can make your life easier and safer by illuminating the path ahead and providing a rear-facing blinker light to help drivers see you in low-light conditions. Bike commuters especially should consider light mounts to make the morning and evening transitions as smooth as possible. Helmet-mounted bike lights work great in conjunction with handlebar-mounted lights because they move with you when you turn your head.

For those who ride during daylight, visors provide a built-in sun shield, especially for mountain bikers or rec riders. Road riders may use a cycling cap under the helmet and eschew any helmet-related extras.

Most modern helmets come equipped with safety technology such as Mips, KinetiCore, Koroyd, and WaveCel.

It has been revealed that these technologies are engineered to help reduce the forces transmitted to your brain from impacts and collisions in different ways. However, no system or technology can guarantee a better outcome in every situation.

When researching a helmet’s protection, consider rotational and direct-impact forces. Choose a lid that uses a time-tested safety system. Look for positive reviews from actual users, not only quotes from brands. Full-spectrum protection might cost more than the most bare-bones helmet, but it’s worth the price for frequent riders and anyone who ventures off the beaten path onto gnarly singletrack or into heavy traffic.

Recent findings suggest that mips (Multi-Directional Impact Protection System) is the most widely know helmet technology. It comes in several versions and is used by numerous helmet brands.The most common Mips tech uses a liner inside the helmet that allows your head and helmet to move relative to each other in the event of a crash. Upon impact, the helmet can move without pulling on your head, which claims to reduce brain trauma. Mips Spherical found on some Giro models is variant. The MIPS SL pads in the Specialized Prevail III is another example.

KinetiCore uses blocks and channels in the helmet’s EPS foam designed to create crumple zones that absorb energy under impact impact.Lazer claims KinetiCore improves ventilation, reduces weight, and limits plastic use in its helmets.

According to recent reports, koroyd uses miniature tubes thermo-welded to create a honeycomb shape. The material crumples in on itself upon impact. Smith typically applies Koroyd in a zonal manner, built into particular places on the helmet to optimize weight and space savings while protecting the most vulnerable parts of your head. Smith’s latest helmet models employ Koroyd and Mips for a double dose of leading-edge protection.

Used in four Trek helmet models, Wavecel is a 15mm-thick grid of layered polyester intended to crumple, flex, and glide on impact. Trek claims this system reduces forces on the rider’s head.

In addition to standard road, mountain, and commuter helmets, some brands offer full-face and e-bike-rated helmets.

Only the Netherlands has an e-bike-specific helmet standard (adopted there in 2017). NTA 8776 is a standard designed to protect against higher-impact speeds and covers a slightly larger part of the head.

Industry observers note that in the U.S., there are at the moment no helmet requirements specific to e-bike use. However, several manufacturers sell commuter helmets built to the NTA 8776 standard. Two of our favorites are the Specialized Mode and the Smith Dispatch MIPS.

Recent findings suggest that the helmets in this story are “half-shells” and cover the top of the head. Their coverage usually ends around the eyebrows and top of the ears, though some—particularly mountain bike helmets—extend to the back of the rider’s head.

Another style of helmet is the full face. As the name suggests, this style covers most of a rider’s head and has a chin bar to protect the rider’s jaw. A full-face helmet covers the ears and the back of the head, with a large opening in front that allows a rider to wear goggles.

In a recent development, full-face helmets protect more of the rider’s head—particularly the mouth and jaw—but are heavier and less ventilated than traditional cycling helmets. Full face helmets are primarily used by mountain bikers—especially downhill and enduro racers—but all riders can benefit from the extra protection they provide.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#171267. 3 Winter Fueling Mistakes You’re Probably Making—and How to Fix Them

3 Winter Fueling Mistakes You’re Probably Making—and How to Fix Them

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling.
  • As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.
  • Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling. Our regular eating schedules shift around social gatherings, holiday menus influence our usual food choices, and staying hydrated can take more effort without higher temperatures to drive our thirst.

As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.

Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.

It has been revealed that vitamin D deficiencies are common among athletes in winter, Maddie Alm, RD, a registered dietitian and the founder of Fueling Forward Sports Nutrition in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. That’s because shorter days and colder temperatures can mean less exposure to the sun’s UVB rays, which help our bodies produce vitamin D.

In a recent development, alm explains that this vitamin not only supports strong bones, but also helps keep our immune and digestive systems functioning at their best. It plays an key role in brain health and mood, too. According to the National Institutes of Health, low blood levels of the vitamin have been associated with a higher risk of depression.

The Fix: Get outside daily to catch some sunshine, and focus on eating more vitamin D–rich foods, with the goal to consume 600 international units (IU) per day.

Good sources of vitamin D include milk, yogurt, cottage cheese, tuna, salmon, egg yolk, and mushrooms. Some cereals and orange juices are also vitamin D–fortified. For reference, three ounces of salmon contain 450 IU, one cup of cow’s milk contains 180 IU, one large egg yolk contains 40 IU, and one cup of fortified cereal contains 40 IU.

It’s a good idea, Alm adds, to check your levels through bloodwork once or twice a year and to consult a professional if your numbers come back low. If you have a hard time hitting your daily quota through food alone, you may benefit from taking a vitamin D supplement.

In a recent development, runners can also overlook vitamin C intake this time of year, claims Sakiko Minagawa, RD, a registered dietitian for the Division of Sports Medicine at Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Ohio and two-time Olympic Marathon Trials qualifier. Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, supports immune health, which is especially key during cold and flu season.

Sources indicate that our bodies also need vitamin C to produce collagen, a protein that’s essential for tissue growth and repair. “While vitamin C may not prevent you from outright getting sick, some research shows that it may decrease the duration of cold symptoms,” Minagawa explains.

The Fix: Up your consumption of foods with vitamin C, such as bell peppers, citrus fruits, greens, and strawberries. Women should aim for 75 milligrams per day, while men should aim for 90 milligrams daily.

You’ll get about 210 milligrams from one large red or orange bell pepper, and 90 milligrams in a cup of raw strawberry halves—each of which achieves your recommended daily dose.

According to recent reports, because vitamin C helps with iron absorption, Minagawa suggests pairing the two whenever possible. Some meals she recommends are a spinach salad with strawberries, an omelet with spinach and red bell peppers, and tomato soup with lentils or black beans.

In the winter, you might not end your run with a dry mouth and sweat-soaked shirt like in the summer, but it’s still critical to hydrate. “Even when it’s cold, you still sweat,” says Minagawa, which means you still need to replenish fluids throughout the day, as well as before and after a workout.

According to recent reports, similarly, your midrun fueling and hydrating remain just as crucial for performance. It’s true: Tearing open an energy gel with gloved hands can pose a real challenge. But, if you’re doing long runs through the colder months, you still need to consume enough carbohydrates during your effort.

The Fix: Minagawa suggests carrying a water bottle that you can easily drink from and refill throughout the day. If you have a hard time sipping on plain water, remember that soups, broths, and hot chocolate can also help you stay hydrated—and can double as recovery fuel.

Don’t forget about fresh fruits and vegetables, either, as they can help with hydration. Some great in-season options that can contribute to your overall fluid intake include grapefruit, clementines, pomegranate, kiwi, squash, Brussels sprouts, sweet potatoes, pears, kale, and cabbage.

During your winter long runs, experiment with fueling options other than energy gels and chews. Some great alternatives you can easily carry in a small plastic baggie include salted Medjool dates, boiled red potatoes, dried fruit, pretzels, and even candy.

Bad weather conditions, scant daylight hours, and more limited racing opportunities make winter a time for many athletes to dial back their training. Taking an off-season can benefit you in the long haul, but Minagawa encourages runners to still stay active—even if that means swapping some runs for walks, bike rides, easy swims, or elliptical sessions.

You don’t want to depart from those year-round healthy habits, Brianna Butler, RD, a registered dietitian, co-owner of Stef & Bri Wellness in Texas, and former professional WNBA athlete, previously told Runner’s World. The same applies to your nutrition.

“The biggest mistake runners make is that, when it’s the off-season, they’re off everything—they say, ‘I’m not doing anything, I’m going to eat whatever’—they’re just winging it,” Butler indicates. “It shouldn’t be all or nothing. We want to make sure we’re nourishing our bodies well year-round.”.

If your training load changes significantly, pay closer attention to your hunger cues to make sure your nutrition matches your energy needs.

The Fix: Maintain a daily exercise routine you enjoy, prioritize nutrient-dense meals and snacks, and resist making drastic changes to your diet.

Industry observers note that if you do find yourself feeling sluggish this time of year, it can be tempting to repent with cleanses, detoxes, and extreme exercise regimens. But such quick fixes rarely pay off in the long run, Alm warns, as they put you at risk for injury, burnout, and subpar seasons to come.

In a recent development, alm notes not to stress if you ditched your typical eating and training schedule for a few weeks and are feeling less energetic as a result. When you return to your usual healthy habits, your body will naturally find its sweet spot. “Trust the process and don’t panic,” Alm advises, because our bodies may change as we move through different training phases. “It is okay to not be at your leanest year-round.”.

The smartest path forward? Do your best to move your body daily, fuel it with what it needs, and give yourself permission to rest when you’re tired. That way, you’ll find yourself feeling strong and ready to train hard again come spring.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

Sources indicate that A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.
